#1300. Lionesses take step closer to World Cup but do not look like they can win it

England may have edged a step closer to booking their place at next summer’s Women’s World Cup but they do not yet look like a team who can win it.

This two-legged qualifying play-off with Greece was always going to be somewhat academic. Greece are ranked 58th in the world and have never qualified for a major tournament. But they could – and should – have taken the lead before England eventually broke the deadlock through Georgia Stanway just before half-time.

The goals flowed more freely in the second half, but Greece deservedly found the net themselves and are not yet out of the tie. There is every chance of the Lionesses winning the second leg in Leicester on Tuesday more comfortably, but not being able to put teams to the sword is exactly why they ended up in the play-offs in the first place.

The best teams are ruthless and unforgiving – and England did not display those traits here. They snatched at chances, and several players were guilty of firing wide. There were also defensive problems. Greece got in behind England’s back line too often and the goal they scored was far too easy for them.

“I think we made it [the game] a bit harder,” England manager Sarina Wiegman said. “Greece were very well prepared. They were very well organised and well disciplined. Of course I’m happy with the 3-1, I’m not happy with the one.

“We could have scored more goals, we should have. The final stage, the final pass needs to be better. I think we were a little bit in moments really good on the ball and in other moments not so good, and we could have made better decisions too. Lots of things to take from today.

“Sometimes we played really well, sometimes we were a bit sloppy, so sometimes we were a bit frustrated and I think that’s what you saw.”

Avoid defeat in the second leg and England will play the winners of Ukraine v Slovakia. Ukraine, whom the Lionesses beat 6-1 and 3-0 earlier in their campaign, have a 3-1 lead from their first leg. Perhaps the pedestrian nature of this game was partly because it felt inevitable England would win. They did enough to get over the line but still lacked a clinical edge.

It had been four months since they were thrashed 4-0 by Spain, a defeat which relegated them to the play-offs instead of automatic qualification. They had won every other game in their group before that capitulation, but with Spain topping the group on goal difference, England only had themselves to blame for not scoring more goals in their other fixtures. Breaking down ultra-defensive teams has long been an issue for this Wiegman side and they knew that was what they would be facing in this double-header against Greece.

It did not help that many of Wiegman’s players have been struggling for form in the Women’s Super League this season. Wiegman was also without the ever-reliable Lucy Bronze, who dropped out of the squad on Thursday because of injury. That meant Maya Le Tissier was handed a start at right-back while Laura Blindkilde Brown was preferred to Jess Park in the No 10 position.

Greece were far more open than many would have expected, with several gaps in their defence for England to exploit. They also created problems for themselves by insisting on playing out from the back.

England thought they had taken the lead in style when goalkeeper Fafailia Petaloti gave the ball away needlessly. Lauren James took advantage of Petaloti being off her line and produced a tremendous lob from 25 yards out. But the forward was offside when she picked up the ball and the goal was ruled out by VAR.

We couldn’t seem to break through in the first half - the keeper was making saves, we hit the woodwork - but the messaging at half-time was just to keep continuing because we were creating opportunities.

”Not to start snatching or taking shots from distance, just trusting in our style of play and our ability to find gaps. We came out for the second half and scored really quickly. It’s just about sticking to the plan and being patient.”

Erica Meg Parkinson, one of England’s new midfielders, was apparently named after Eric Cantona.

While Cantona still famously is proud of his kung fu kick, when he attacked an obnoxious Crystal Palace fan, Parkison is less enthused by football’s most famous case of breaking the fourth wall.

“My dad is a huge Man United fan so I was named after Eric Cantona,” Parkinson says. “It’s a pretty good player to be named after except for, you know, the karate kicks.

“My brother was named after Denis Law. I don’t think my mum had much of a say in the name so she was dragged into it, but it kind of worked out because we both play football now.”

Hello from sunny Heraklion. It’s very calm here at the moment, with just under 50 minutes to go until kick-off.

Over 500 England fans have made the journey. There may in fact end up being more away fans than home supporters here. Tickets for all fans were free but as it stands, the locals are outnumbered.

It looks as though the Lionesses will set up in a 4-3-3 with Maya Le Tissier coming in at right back for the injured Lucy Bronze.

Greece XI: Petaloti, Giannaka, Paterna, Markou, Gkouni-Papaioannou, Drakogiannaki, Brame, Moraitou, Papatheodorou, Brookshire, Sarri.

Subs: Giannakouli, Katerfiannaki, Ntarzanou, Theodoraki, Kapnisi, Chalatsogianni, Tzourtzevits, Saich, Rapani, Pouliou, Tsela, Kongouli.

England XI: Hampton, Le Tissier, Morgan, Williamson, Greenwood, Walsh, Stanway, Blindkilde Brown, Russo, James, Hemp.

Subs: Charles, Keating, Potter, Carter, Fisk, Park, Mead, Parkinson, Moorhouse, Godfrey, Toone.

Our #Lionesses in Crete 🦁 🙌 https://t.co/qv4VnAgKiM

The excellent Kathryn Batte has run the rule over potential alternatives to Lucy Bronze.

The 35-year-old right-back is out injured, but Ella Toone was called up in her place, rather than a direct replacement.

“Bronze, who is two appearances away from reaching 150 caps for her country, has picked up an injury and returned to Chelsea for treatment,” Batte writes.

“The Lionesses will be missing one of their most reliable players for the matches on Friday and Tuesday, but it gives Sarina Wiegman an opportunity to look at potential replacements for the future.

“Bronze, who has been an integral member of the team throughout Wiegman’s reign, turns 35 later this month. While she will be expected to be the first-choice right-back should England qualify for next year’s World Cup in Brazil, the lack of a recognised back-up has been an ongoing problem.”

Sarina Wiegman revealed that while dropping Toone was a difficult decision, the midfielder’s reaction left a lasting impression on the coaching staff.

“When I gave her the call, of course that was a hard call, but she took that straight away,” Wiegman said. “Of course she was very disappointed, but the first thing she did was say: ‘OK, I’m going to get back, I’m going to do that.’”Wiegman was particularly pleased with how Toone handled herself both on the pitch and in front of the media before her late recall.

“That answer in the game, also the way she spoke about it, I thought that was really good,” the head coach added. “And then getting everything ready, I think that really impressed me. Well done, I would say.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Greece vs England in the first leg of the 2027 Women’s World Cup play-offs.

The Lionesses kick off the two-legged tie tonight looking to secure a solid advantage ahead of Tuesday’s return tie at Leicester’s King Power Stadium. Although they finished level on points with group winners Spain, England’s goal difference sent them into the play-off path, setting up a first-ever senior meeting against a Greek side ranked 55 places below them in the FIFA rankings.

All eyes are on Sarina Wiegman’s selection choices following a turbulent week of squad news. The manager originally raised eyebrows last month by dropping Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly, stating bluntly that “the levels weren’t what I expect from them on the pitch.”

Toone quickly accepted the setback. Speaking after starting in Manchester United’s victory over Liverpool, the midfielder insisted: “It’s about me now. I’ve got to keep working hard and use it as fuel to come back even better.”

That opportunity arrived sooner than expected. An injury sustained by right-back Lucy Bronze - described by Wiegman as “really small” - forced the defender to return to Chelsea for assessment. Wiegman immediately turned to Toone, who flew directly to Greece from Spain, where she had been running her own self-directed training block during the international window.

With 69 caps and 24 international goals to her name - including crucial strikes in the Euro 2022 final and the 2023 World Cup semi-final - Toone brings proven big-match experience back into the setup at a critical moment.

We will bring you all the build-up, confirmed team news, and live play-by-play coverage throughout the evening.

Guardiola attended Oasis' homecoming gig at Heaton Park earlier this year â the bandâs first show on home turf since 2009 â with his daughter Maria. #1298. Designing dislocation-driven polar vortex networks in twisted perovskites

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Twisting two atomic layers produces a geometric moiré pattern but bonding-induced interfacial reconstruction fundamentally transforms this into an ordered dislocation network—a distinction obscured in weakly bonded van der Waals systems. Although in-plane topological vortex nanostructures arising from twisting-induced lateral strain modulation have been linked to periodic moiré patterns in freestanding perovskite layers1,2,3 and 2D bilayers4, their coupling to the interfacial dislocation network in twisted layers remains unresolved. Here we demonstrate that twisted freestanding SrTiO3 (STO) layers undergo interfacial reconstruction into a network of screw dislocations, accompanied by the emergence of in-plane topological vortices. Unlike in previous reports, these vortices are associated with the dislocation network rather than with geometric moiré patterns. Four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4DSTEM) reveals a beam deflection texture in registry with the interfacial dislocation network. A machine learning interatomic potential, trained on first-principles calculations, together with phase-field modelling, confirms that competing strains within the dislocation network stabilize polar vortex–antivortex pairs; first-principles calculations further reveal the emergence of an electronic superlattice with a well-defined periodicity. Our results establish twist-controlled dislocation networks as a new and versatile route to designing local polar and electronic structures in oxide materials.

a,b, The reconstructed 5° twisted interface maximizes Ti coordination in b compared with the rigid structure in a. This reconstruction favours fully coordinated Ti sites (CN = 6, pink and beige) by minimizing undercoordinated Ti regions (CN = 5, yellow and green). This induces a dislocation (shaded grey region) between the two undercoordinated stackings. The insets on the right depict atomic positions across the interface for a central unit cell, illustrating the coordination environment.

Unit-cell averaged εxx, εyy and εxy (from left to right) using the described nearest-neighbour scheme for the TiO2-terminated and SrO-terminated layers (from top to bottom, respectively).

a, MLIP-DFT relaxed atomic positions at a 5° twist showing Ti atoms in the top (light) and bottom (dark) interfacial layers, demonstrating the orthogonal screw dislocation network, with a magnified view on the right. b, Twist-angle dependence of the interface energy (blue) together with the computed and analytical dislocation lengths (orange). The background colour denotes the transition from well-defined dislocations to their absence. c–f, Dislocation lengths are measured using the interlayer distance as a signature. The analytical prediction given by d = (a/2)/sin(θ/2) (orange line) matches the measured dislocation lengths.

a–d, HAADF-STEM image of the (110) cross-section of 7.5° (a,b) and 10° (c,d) twisted samples. Top and bottom images are independently sampled fields of view. The measured dislocation spacing d2 is 2.1 ± 0.2 nm in a,b and 1.5 ± 0.2 nm in c,d, agreeing well with the predictions for d2 = d/√2, as expected from this cross-section viewing plane (see text).

Phase-field model predicted polarization components Px, Py and Pz in blue, green and black, respectively, plotted as a function of the out-of-plane coordinate z in the 5° twisted bicrystal sampled at different positions (denoted by shapes). The middle panel shows these points of interest overlaid on the dislocation network. The interface plane is located at z = 0 nm.

a, PDOS (left) and charge density isosurfaces at Ev − 0.3 eV (right) for a twist angle of 6.7°. b, Zoom-out of a but with isosurfaces at Ev − 0.06 eV highlighting dislocation node detail. The PDOS is further decomposed into node, dislocation line and bulk-like contributions.

#1296. Declan Rice agrees new five-year Arsenal contract: Star to join Bukayo Saka as Gunners' highest-paid player at over £350,000-per-week... with goalkeeper David Raya set to sign long-term deal to stay too

Published: 18:09 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 11:58 EST, 17 November 2026

Declan Rice has agreed a new five-year deal at Arsenal that will run until the summer of 2031 - with goalkeeper David Raya set to join him in committing his future to the club.

The England midfielder is expected to sign the new contract soon, which is set to put him alongside Bukayo Saka as Arsenal's top earner. Saka is on a deal worth over £350,000 a week.

And Raya, 31, is understood to have agreed a deal in principle to extend his terms. Both players' existing deals expire in 2028.

Rice joined Arsenal in 2023 for £105million from West Ham and has established himself as the fulcrum of their midfield, helping steer them to the Premier League title last season.

The 27-year-old played 55 games in all competitions last season as the Gunners reached their first Champions League final since 2006, but lost out to Paris Saint-Germain.

His contract talks have been ongoing from at least March and are now finalised.

Raya joined Arsenal from Brentford on loan in the same summer, and signed a permanent deal a year later.

Declan Rice has agreed a new-five year deal at Arsenal that will run until the summer of 2031

David Raya has agreed a deal in principle to stay on, with his current deal expiring in 2028

Rice had confirmed a new deal was close over the weekend when speaking on international duty with England.

'I've been extremely lucky that I've managed to play at such a consistent level throughout my career.

'I've always been stable in the clubs I've been at.

'A new contract is hopefully on the horizon soon.

'I'm extremely lucky that I'm at a club like Arsenal, where my manager [Mikel Arteta] and my team-mates put so much energy in me.

'I'm extremely lucky I don't have to think about that stuff.'

There will be some games where Mikel Arteta has no choice but to tweak the XI, rest some tired legs and give his second-choice attackers the chance – although given the option he may wish to pick the same team every week.

That was a superb finish from Jurrien Timber who, with two touches, demonstrated that in the modern era even defenders are capable of the kind of moments of skill and composure that we once assumed were only within the capacity of the best attackers. He gave Arsenal the lead just as Mikel Arteta had decided he had seen enough from some of his second-choice attackers – Viktor Gyokeres, Noni Madueke and Mikel Merino. They had created some chances and at times looked promising, but as soon as the big three were on the difference was obvious.

Lille are considering legal ⁠action after defender Tiago Santos suffered a serious knee injury following an “uncontrolled and dangerous” tackle in Saturday’s match ‌against Le Havre.

Santos, 24, suffered a ruptured anterior cruciate ligament and meniscal tear in his right knee and was carried off the pitch on a stretcher after being tackled by Le Havre midfielder Amir Richardson during the first half of Lille’s 1-0 victory.

The referee gave a foul for the tackle but did not issue Richardson with a caution.

Lille said the ‌tackle merited ‌a red card ⁠and that they had asked the league’s governing body (LFP) to refer the matter to its disciplinary committee. The club are also seeking an explanation of ⁠the video review process undertaken by match officials.

“LOSC is exploring all possible legal avenues and reserves the right to take any legal action necessary to obtain compensation for its losses,” the ​club said. “It will support Tiago in ‌any steps he decides to take to defend his rights.”

Arsenal pay tribute to one of the club’s greatest custodians this evening following the news of Ken Friar’s death aged 92. Friar worked in various roles at the club across more than 70 years, and a bridge from Drayton Park to Emirates Stadium is named in his honour.

A statue at the end of the bridge is a nod to the chance meeting the 11-year-old Friar had with Arsenal manager George Allison in 1945, while playing football outside Highbury with his friends.

As Sam Dean wrote earlier today, finishing the story: “Allison was so impressed by Friar’s enthusiasm that he told him to report to his office at 9am the next day. Friar did as he was instructed and his reward was a job offer: he became a messenger at the stadium on match days. He was paid 12 and a half pence per week.”

Friar was a long-serving member of the Arsenal board, before stepping back in 2020 and becoming life president.

Arsenal’s home record in the Champions League has been formidable since they returned to the competition under Arteta in 2023. They have won all 11 home group-stage or league-phase matches, conceding just three goals (two of those were shipped against Kairat Almaty in a dead rubber).

Arteta’s scope for rotation has been reduced by injuries to Piero Hincapie and Martin Zubimendi, but tonight’s game should offer Eberechi Eze and Viktor Gyokeres a chance to impress, while Jurrien Timber needs minutes to build his fitness.

#1291. Chasing dynasty: How Gotham FC's NWSL Shield win completes transformation ahead of playoffs

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

En route to their second NWSL championship in two years, relatively new Gotham FC recruit Jaedyn Shaw was uninterested in the narratives that underestimated her team. The surprise win at the NWSL Shield-winning Kansas City Current in the playoff quarterfinals was not a surprise to her, and she made it clear with three quick words: "Underdog, my ass."

Shaw had a point on that cold day in the Midwest, and almost exactly a year later, it still stands. Gotham are the NWSL's new dynasty, and their Shield win marked their fifth major title in three years, with a sixth in their sights as the playoffs begin this weekend. The transformation was rapid for a team that has historically been a bottom-dweller, so much so that their 2023 championship triumph was a genuine surprise. They quickly built a title-winning team and reaped the rewards just as swiftly, but even as the muscle memory of title charges returns, Gotham will go about their next NWSL playoff journey differently. The target is officially on their backs, the onus officially on them to live up to the billing.

Gotham have played the vast majority of their playoff games as the lowest-seeded team in the postseason, winning the championship twice in those circumstances. Sunday's quarterfinal against the Seattle Reign, though, will be the first game they play as the unquestionable favorites to win the whole thing. How Gotham will play with the weight of expectations is entirely unclear, since they have never done it before, but it is a good problem of their own creation, one they have chased since the 2023 triumph.

Date: Sunday, Nov. 8 | Time: 12:30 p.m. ETLocation: Sports Illustrated Stadium -- Harrison, N.J.TV: ABC | Live stream: ESPN AppOdds: Gotham FC -150; Draw +265; Seattle Reign +340

Their blitz in the free-agent market in the winter of 2024 laid the foundation for their dynastic run, but the most fascinating feature of Gotham's years-long run of success is the evolution they have undergone since. U.S. women's national team defender Tierna Davidson has become the team's captain, her progressive passing ability making her a key fixture in head coach Juan Carlos Amoros' system. Her club and country teammate Rose Lavelle has become a standout, but the star of the show has been Shaw, who has barely missed a beat since her arrival in September 2025.

Shaw has 14 goals and seven assists in 35 NWSL games with Gotham, her wide-ranging skill set fully on display in Amoros' team. She has been a little bit of everything for the team's attack, which is arguably too reliant on her talents, but it is almost hard to fault Amoros for the approach. The system has allowed Shaw to flourish, in particular bringing out a clear goal-scoring quality that is key to a Gotham team that values defensive work rate first.

"First, I think the commitment they have to defend and the commitment they have to work hard for the team despite being some of the best players technically in the planet," Amoros said about both Shaw and Lavelle after a win over the Chicago Stars in September. "I think that helps the connection, not only between them two. There is a mutual respect there because of that but then also from the whole team. When you have to play and those are the players that produce the chances for us in the final third but then the people that [are] behind them are always supportive of them because of the work they put in and then we try to work a lot with them to how we can find them and how they can connect more with each other and the same with Sam [Kerr]."

He has found a unique way to make Shaw and Lavelle work together, despite the fact that they appear to have overlapping skill sets when it comes time for USWNT head coach Emma Hayes to slot them into her lineup. The pair often play just behind Kerr, an out-and-out striker, and assume the role of strikers themselves while balancing their creative tendencies. They have filled in some gaps along the way -- Kerr, for example, ranks third in the league with 9.67 expected goals since returning to the NWSL on July 16 but has scored just four times. Kerr does, though, have four assists in 17 games, one fewer than Shaw and one more than Lavelle over that span.

The connection between Lavelle and Shaw has offered Gotham a level of dynamism that has been missing in their attack at times over the years, even as they racked up title after title. It helps that the two have enjoyed working alongside each other, the 21-year-old Shaw in particular taking inspiration from Lavelle, a decade her senior.

"I think her movement is some of the best in the world, honestly," Shaw said after that September win over the Stars. "She's able to make stretch runs, drag players. She attracts so many players, opening up space for other players to get on the ball and then getting on the second one, I think, is one of her strengths and is something I'm trying to replicate off of her. I think she's just incredibly smart in soccer knowledge."

For each of them, a return to fitness after small injuries in the final weeks of the regular season comes not a moment too soon. Kerr's inconsistency is not the only attacking issue they will need to overcome -- Jordyn Dudley will miss the postseason with a foot fracture she sustained last month, her impressive rookie season coming to a close with four goals and three assists. Lavelle and Shaw will be particularly useful against the Reign, whose defensive qualities continue to be a strength.

Shaw has become the focal point of Gotham's reinvention in recent years, but Amoros' side has added experienced options in a wide variety of positions since the 2023 championship. The vast majority of Gotham's likely starters on Sunday will have joined the club after the 2023 playoff run, a steady stream of important players signing themselves up since. Ann-Katrin Berger, the 2024 goalkeeper of the year, made the move not long after Davidson and Lavelle did, and European champion Jess Carter followed right after. Midfielder Jaelin Howell, who has been in and around the USWNT, was recruited in time for the 2025 season, and Shaw joined months later. Left back Guro Reiten has two goals and six assists since making her club debut in April, while Kerr made the move at roughly the same time as midfielder Denise O'Sullivan, a two-time NWSL champion with the North Carolina Courage.

Gotham's reinvention is constant, the core evolving each and every season. It is a unique route to the top, but in another season of change, they found the consistency they have been chasing since the 2023 championship. The underdog label has well and truly been shed, the team chasing another tag entirely -- a third championship would put them level with the Portland Thorns as the most successful team in the league's history.

Gary Neville has stood up for under-fire Manchester United man Diogo Dalot – and named three of his defensive team-mates he would rather see leave the club before him.

Gary Neville has defended Man United star Diogo Dalot - arguing that he has team-mates who are far weaker

The Portugal international has come in for heavy criticism from supporters this season

But in his opinion, there are three defenders that he would let go in the 'first wave' of changes in Manchester.

'Physically what will happen is with Yoro, he'll go one way or the other. I like the fact he's been brought into the French team. It tells me sometimes you just have got to connect the dots and think, "okay, well, if they think he's good, then we must be missing something here because we're not seeing it yet, are we?".'

Neville went on to suggest that Yoro was lacking the connection within his body that Premier League rivals such as Jeremy Jacquet are already able to harness – something Sir Alex Ferguson had identified in Rio Ferdinand when he was at West Ham.

Alan Shearer says there has been improvement tonight since Saturday. “They have stuck together and have not been outrun.” This is a very low bar but OK. He goes on to say that the glaring weakness is not attitude but a lack of finishing quality.

And Le Normand is booked within seconds of his introduction for a tug of the shirt.

Dalot lofts a deep cross way beyond Zirkzee. I think Dalot encompasses Man Utd’s recruitment over the past eight years or so in that it’s hard to see any progression or improvement since the day they signed him. Maybe he always had a low ceiling. But where on earth is the coaching?

Manchester United have had their chances but they have lacked an elite or even merely decent finisher.

Atletico 2 Man Utd 0 (Lookman)  The three men were not enough and were carved apart by one pass from the left, from Grimaldo I think to David who opened his body to fire a shot towards the bottom right. Lammens dives to save but Lookman is Johnny on the spot to beat Dalot to the rebound and score.

Carrick now has three at the back after the sending off.

He places his hand on his shoulder and let it creep down on to Lookman’s chest as the former Everton winger tried to run clear from 40 yards.

The referee is sent to the screen to look again at Yoro’s contact on Lookman, the hand on the shoulder. Was it DOGSO, denial of a goalscoring opportunity. It was very weak.

Fernandes plays the corner to Amad standing to the left of the D, who rolls it halfway back and the captain wraps his foot around a blistering shot that thumps into the crossbar.

Cute pass from Heaven sends Amad down the left but still no target for him to find and he has to settle for a corner.

Mount wins the ball off Baena, passes out to Dalot on the right and he squares it to Bruno Fernandes. The captain opens his foot to shoot and the ball deflects off Zirkzee, killing its power. Oblak flops forward to gather.

Amad is on the left, Mbeumo to the right and Zirkzee down the middle with Fernandes tucked behind.

After Baena shoots at Lammens, Man Utd make a triple substitution:

Amad → RashfordMount → BalebaZirkzee → Tielemans.

Cross from the right. Bruno whips it around the left-back but Mbeumo, not really a centre-forward, held his line rather than running across Romero’s shoulder and that allows the former Spurs captain to get there first. Bruno signals his frustration.

Pubill goes to right-back and Llorente moves into midfield.

Baena cuts in off the left to shoot with his right, trying to curl it into the top right but the ball will not bend to his will and ends up being far to straight. He was looking for a banana bend and ended up with a cucumber.

Manchester United carve Atletico open with a simple long, left to right diagonal pass that Romero misjudges. Fernandes leaps to try to hook it on the volley over Oblak but instead steers it wide of the left post.

Terrific pass from Barrios picks out Alvarez on the left of the box and he thumps his shot into the post. Lammens, who dived to try to stop it, is stranded but Martinez is there to scramble the ball behind as it rebounded into the six-yard box.

Rashford slips Tielemans down the left and he stands up a cross that Oblan can pick out of the sky unmolested. Might be worth a gamble if they had Sesko to bring on.

Baena arrows a long cross straight at Lammens.

Good work from Baleba to win the ball off Barrios as the arrowhead of a three-man press but his chip down the left finds Rashford offside.

A foul on Fernandes is followed 40 seconds later by Rashford being penalised for trying to get past Simeone by holding his shoulder.

Yoro pushes high into the press and dispossesses Grimaldo and squares it to Bruno Fernandes. He clips a pass towards the penalty spot but too far from Mbeumo. Fernandes is patently unfit. I know he’s the captain/talisman but he is not very effective tonight.

No doubt Manchester United have improved and created a couple of chances for Mbeumo and one for Rashford. Baleba should really have buried that free back-post header from the corner, too. And that second Atletico ‘goal’ being disallowed was a real tonic on the stroke of half-time. Kudos fro not crumbling. But I wouldn’t be surprised if Baena, Alvarez and Lee carved them open again.

Atletico have a free-kick on the right just inside the Man Utd half for Heaven’s shove. They go back to switch it up the left, then back over to the right.

United have settled down a little now after that horrific start and they’ve fashioned good chances for Mbeumo and Rashford. There’s that feeling, though, that Atletico could just run through the gears at any moment. Some of their movement is so good.

Bruno Fernandes scoops a cross from the right to the back post. Man Utd are outnumbered 6-2 in the Atletico box and Simeone calmly chests it back to the seemingly ageless Oblak.

One downside of this front three is that they are allowing, by design, I think, Atletico’s central defenders to stroke the ball around without putting them under any pressure.

The rotation of Atletico’s forwards – Baena, Alvarez, Lee and Simeone – is dragging the Man Utd defenders out of position. They still need more help from Baleba and Santos.

Vast improvement in the last few minutes from the away side and now Martinez wedges a chip over Romero and Llorente into the path of Rashford’s superb run. Mbeumo sprays a pass up the left for Rashford to chase and he lengthens his stride into a gallop. But Llorente is just as quick, stalks his every step and makes the tackle.

Baena, Johnny and Barrios zip passes between them in a triangle to take Dalot out of the game but back comes Santos to block Baena’s cross.

Baena has the freedom of the field and Man Utd are not picking him up. He drops off Santos to shoot from 20 yards but Yoro gets in the way. He ghosts into space and with Grimaldo pushing high on the left also, he’s too much for Dalot to handle.

Could not have got off to a worse start. No doubt the lack of understanding between the players contributed to that mix-up.

Or, finally, that it’s 4-2-3-1 with the trident of Rashford, Tielemans and Bruno.

This feels a big moment for Carrick and United’s players to answer some of their critics. They have been getting battered from all sides in the last couple of days. Nicky Butt suggested on his podcast that Carrick told him before he got the United job that management “not for me” and “my head’s all over the shop” and that United was the only job he would take. At the very least, those comments are unhelpful and they are thought to have been dimly received internally.

Jamie Carragher offered a lacerating analysis of United’s performance against Spurs on Saturday on Sky Sports on Monday night and suggested things could get “very messy, very quickly” for all involved if there is not marked improvement. Steven Gerrard questioned why United opted to invest £50m of their summer budget in Andrey Santos, an unused substitute in the last three league games, insisted the back four was not good enough and questioned the work ethic.

And it was interesting to see Carrick alongside his mate Wayne Rooney just now pitchside. Rooney told the Stick to United podcast that captain Bruno Fernandes looks “fed up” and ready to explode at any moment.

It would have been pretty unthinkable for Carrick not to run with a three-man midfield here, not just because of the wide open spaces opponents have exploited this season but when you look at the back line United are fielding. Dalot at left back, two youngsters in Lenny Yoro and Ayden Heaven and a horribly out of form Lisandro Maríinez.

Nor has Senne Lammens looked convincing this term. Matheus Cunha has been dropped – not before time – and I expect to see Fernandes playing off the right. There’s going to a big onus on Rashford on the left. I’m not sure if he is fully fit but he’s going to be important.

It’s fantastic. It’s where we want to be, these games, these competitions. It’s as tough a place as you can come to. They’ve got a really good history in this competition and it’s where we want to come to challenge and test ourselves. We have put ourselves in this position, got a good start at home and now this is our first away game.

We want a reaction, of course. A positive reaction [to Saturday’s poor performance]. It hasn’t gone how we wanted, how we expected so far but it’s been fine margins in some of those games. It can go both ways but the reality is where we are at now.

It’s a fresh night and we’ve got to adapt, we’ve got to adjust in a positive way.

We want a little more control in the game [with three central midfielders]. At times we have been too open. We wanted to make a difference in that way. We’ve made other changes, certain spaces, certain positions.

To be honest it’s not really a big change of shape, personnel maybe but a lot of it is similar. We want more control, a little bit without the ball and a lot more with it. We’re happy with the way we set up.

Look at the last three goals we’ve conceded. They’re a mixed bag, simple goals you can something about. We need to defend better as a whole team .

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Atlético Madrid and Manchester United from the Metropolitano. The two sides had contrasting fortunes in their opening fixtures in this competition, Man Utd beating Azerbaijan’s Sabah 4-0 at Old Trafford a month ago while Atléti were defeated by Liverpool who came back from 1-0 down to win 2-1.

But domestically it is the other way round – Michael Carrick’s side have made the club’s worst start in the league for 40 years with one win, three draws and two defeats and have been knocked out of the League Cup. Those of us who watch them regularly – purely because of occupational obligations in this instance – have been surprised by how poor they have been. The results have been bad but the performances even worse.

They seem to lack players who can play on the front foot, who have the athletic dynamism required in this league and too many self-indulgent forward players who either can’t be bothered to help out their team-mates or cannot concentrate long enough to do so. Spooked by their lack of pace in defence and midfield, they are hidebound by caution, dropping ever deeper, ever more reliant on counter-attacking despite the blatant disconnect between the front four and back six. If they drift through this match and Sunday’s trip to Elland Road, Carrick may join the long list of Ineos-driven managerial mis-steps.

Atlético have won six of eight in La Liga and have been defeated only once. They are five points behind Barcelona in second and have score 18 goals and let in eight, which may seem a curious thing to include in a preview but it is done to emphasise that many fans’ perception of Diego Simeone’s team are out of date. Back in the days of Diego Godín, Gabi, Juanfran et all, six wins a draw and a defeat would have had goals for of about 10 and goals against of maybe three.

Simeone is a martinet about attitude not systems or styles and his team have evolved, with the World Cup-winner Alex Baena, who has scored four goals so far, driving them on. He has reintegrated Julián Alvarez, too, after his brazen attempt to force a move to Barcelona so incensed Atléti fans that it seemed they would drive him out of the club. Simeone refused to let Alvarez get his own way and he is now buckling down. Ten years ago Simeone would have bitten his head off.

The one surviving veteran in the squad from that first of El Cholo’s Liga winning sides and the two Champions League finals, victory in which would represent Simeone’s crowning achievement, is the midfielder Koke. Remarkably, if he features today, the 34-year-old midfielder will be making his 750th first-team appearance as an Atlético player.

#1287. Evidence for p-wave magnetism in electronic band structure of metallic EuSi

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

One active frontier of quantum-matter research is the realization of p-wave symmetry-breaking phases in fermionic systems, long exemplified by the A phase of superfluid helium-3 (refs. 1,2,3). Achieving p-wave superconductivity4 and its magnetic analogue5—characterized by a time-reversal-symmetric, p-wave spin-polarized Fermi surface—remains a grand challenge6,7. Despite recent progress in identifying candidate p-wave magnets5,7,8,9,10, spin-resolved spectroscopic evidence for their electronic structures remains limited. Here we report angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and spin-ARPES evidence for p-wave magnetism in the near-Fermi-level electronic structure of stoichiometric metallic EuSi, supported by symmetry analysis, first-principles calculations and neutron scattering. Neutron diffraction reveals a chiral spiral phase between 33.4 K and 62 K that fulfils archetypal p-wave magnetism criteria: it preserves the combined symmetry of time reversal and lattice translation, while breaking inversion symmetry. Spin-integrated ARPES reveals a pronounced magnetism-driven reconstruction of the electronic structure, with energy separations exceeding 100 meV, and spin-ARPES resolves Sy polarization in near-Fermi-level spectral features. The extracted Sy exhibits a sign-changing modulation across successive magnetic Brillouin zones and is suppressed near the nodal regions, consistent with the predicted p-wave spin texture and unfolded spin-polarization calculations. Magnetic force microscopy and micro-ARPES further reveal approximately 10-μm chiral magnetic domains. These results identify EuSi as a stoichiometric metallic platform for investigating p-wave magnetism in electronic band structures and spin-symmetry-based functionalities in spintronics10, topological matter7, superconductivity11 and beyond.

Unconventional symmetry breaking in itinerant fermion systems has revealed some of the most remarkable phases of quantum matter. A celebrated example is p-wave superfluidity in helium-3, where odd-parity Cooper pairing generates emergent orders beyond conventional paradigms1,2,3. Its magnetic analogue, the p-wave magnet, is characterized by an odd-parity spin-polarized electronic structure that preserves the combined symmetry of time reversal and lattice translation while breaking inversion symmetry5,6.

Recently, spin group theory has provided a framework for identifying such magnetic states5, extending concepts developed for altermagnets12. Whereas ferromagnets exhibit conventional s-wave-like spin splitting and altermagnets exhibit even-parity d-, g- or i-wave spin order12,13, p-wave magnets are characterized by odd-parity spin polarization associated with commensurate coplanar magnetic order that breaks inversion symmetry while preserving a combined time-reversal and translation symmetry5,14. The resulting electronic structure can exhibit a single symmetry-allowed spin component, symmetry-enforced nodal planes and a characteristic momentum-dependent spin texture. Candidate p-wave magnetism has recently been explored in insulating NiI2 (ref. 8) and metallic Gd3(Ru1−δRhδ)4Al12 (ref. 9). However, spin-resolved spectroscopic evidence for the characteristic odd-parity electronic spin texture remains limited8,9.

Here we present evidence for p-wave magnetism in the near-Fermi-level (near-EF) electronic structure of stoichiometric metallic EuSi by combining symmetry analysis, first-principles calculations, neutron scattering and photoemission spectroscopy. Neutron diffraction reveals a commensurate spiral phase with propagation vector (0, 1/3, 0) below the upper magnetic transition temperature, TN1 ≈ 62 K, followed by a transition to a conical phase at the lower magnetic transition temperature, TN2 ≈ 33.4 K. Magnetotransport measurements indicate strong coupling between magnetism and itinerant electrons. Below TN1, spin-integrated angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) reveals a pronounced magnetism-driven reconstruction of the electronic structure, with energy separations exceeding 100 meV, associated with strong 4f–5d exchange coupling. Spin-ARPES provides spin-resolved spectroscopic evidence for the expected odd-parity Sy polarization in the near-EF spectral features: the extracted polarization changes sign across successive magnetic Brillouin zones and is suppressed near the nodal regions, consistent with the predicted p-wave spin texture and unfolded spin-polarization calculations. Because the near-EF spin-resolved features contain contributions from multiple folded bands with momentum-dependent spectral weights, the observed Sy modulation is best interpreted as a spectroscopic signature of the expected p-wave spin texture at the level of the reconstructed electronic structure. Magnetic force microscopy (MFM) and micro-ARPES further reveal approximately 10-µm chiral magnetic domains. Together, these observations identify EuSi as a stoichiometric metallic platform for investigating p-wave magnetism in electronic band structures and related spin-symmetry-based phenomena.

In conventional ferromagnets and altermagnets (Fig. 1a), broken time-reversal symmetry permits even-parity spin-polarized electronic structures12. In the non-relativistic limit, conventional ferromagnets exhibit s-wave-like spin splitting, whereas altermagnets can exhibit d-, g- or i-wave-like spin-splitting patterns12,13,15,16,17,18. By contrast, unconventional odd-parity magnets can host p-, f- or h-wave spin polarization that preserves time-reversal (\(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}\))-related symmetry while breaking inversion (\(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{P}}\)) symmetry5. Commensurate chiral magnetic structures provide a natural route to such \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{P}}\)-symmetry breaking. In particular, coplanar non-collinear exchange fields can generate odd-parity spin polarization in momentum space when the magnetic structure preserves the combined symmetry of time reversal and lattice translation, \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}{\boldsymbol{\tau }}\) (ref. 5). As in conventional antiferromagnets, this symmetry enforces zero net magnetization in the ideal p-wave magnetic state (Fig. 1a).

a, Schematic magnetic orders and their associated s-wave (ferromagnetic), d-wave (altermagnetic) and p-wave spin splitting in momentum space. Magenta and cyan spheres represent magnetic atoms with opposite spin orientations, related by the indicated combined spin–space symmetry operations in the d- and p-wave states, whereas blue spheres represent nonmagnetic atoms. b, Spiral magnetic structure of EuSi. The characteristic p-wave spin group symmetries are spin rotation combined with a glide mirror plane \([{C}_{2z}{||}{M}_{y}{\bf{t}}]\), and with a lattice translation \([{C}_{2}{||}{\bf{t}}]\), respectively. c, Calculated spin-polarized Fermi surface of the spiral phase, including SOC, showing p-wave spin polarization and spin splitting. d, Calculated spin textures near the top of the valence bands in the kz = 0 (bottom) and kx = 0 (top) planes, with (left) and without (right) SOC. e, Calculated spin-polarized band dispersion along the −Ym–Г–Ym (ky) direction in the spiral phase, with (left) and without (right) SOC. f, Conical magnetic structure of EuSi, with the combined spin-rotation and translation symmetry \([{C}_{6}{||}{{\bf{t}}}^{{\prime} }]\) indicated. g, Calculated spin-polarized band dispersions along the same momentum direction in the conical phase, with (left) and without (right) SOC.

We next consider the symmetry of the experimentally determined magnetic structures of EuSi. The crystal belongs to the point group D2h (space group Cmcm), and its magnetic states without (with) considering the effect of spin–orbit coupling (SOC) are described by the corresponding spin (magnetic) space group7. For the spiral state below TN1 ≈ 62 K, the spin space group is \({{}^{{2}_{y}}C}^{1}{m}^{{m}_{x}}{c}^{1}{m}^{{m}_{y}}1\), which satisfies the criteria for collinear p-wave spin polarization in momentum space. The spin space group breaks the \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{P}}\) symmetry, thereby allowing odd-parity spin polarization. The coplanarity of the magnetic moments, together with the spin-only symmetry \({C}_{2y}{\mathcal{T}}=[{M}_{y}|1]\,{=}^{{m}_{y}}1\), constrains the spin polarization to the y direction in momentum space. Combined with the \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}{\boldsymbol{\tau }}\) symmetry, the spin group symmetry prohibits the spin components Sx and Sz, while allowing a \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}\)-symmetric Sy component satisfying:

The spin-degenerate nodal plane at ky = 0, where ky is the component of the electron crystal momentum k = (kx, ky, kz) along the reciprocal-space direction corresponding to the crystallographic b axis, is protected by the combined spin rotation, lattice mirror and translation symmetry \([{C}_{2z}{||}{M}_{y}t]\), as illustrated in Fig. 1b. The corresponding spin-polarized electronic-structure calculations are shown in Fig. 1c–e. Figure 1d illustrates the calculated p-wave spin–momentum locking near the top of the valence band in the (kx, ky, 0) and (0, ky, kz) planes. The calculated bands obey the symmetry relations:

Here, E(kx,ky,kz,Sy) denotes the electronic band energy at crystal momentum k for a state with spin polarization Sy along the b direction. Comparison of calculations with and without SOC (Fig. 1c–e) shows that the characteristic p-wave spin polarization and splitting arise predominantly from the non-relativistic magnetic exchange, with only minor modifications from SOC. These calculations therefore provide the symmetry and electronic-structure framework for the p-wave state expected from the spin and magnetic (\({P}_{C}{2}_{1}{2}_{1}{2}_{1}\)) space groups of the experimentally determined spiral magnetic structure.

We next consider the conical state below TN2 ≈ 33.4 K. Its spin space group takes the ferromagnetic form \({{}^{{2}_{y}}C}^{1}{m}^{{m}_{x}}{c}^{1}{m}^{{6}_{y}}{t}^{{\prime} }\), characterized by a symmetry combining a six-fold spin rotation with translation, [\({C}_{6y}{|}{t}^{{\prime} }\)], as shown in Fig. 1f. Figure 1g shows the calculated electronic structure without and with SOC. The calculated dispersions of the spiral and conical phases are similar over much of momentum space but differ near the Γ point (Fig. 1e,g). In the conical phase, broken \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}\) lifts the spin degeneracy at the Γ point that is protected in the spiral phase (see Supplementary Note 1 for further symmetry analysis). Accordingly, an anomalous Hall response is symmetry-allowed in the conical phase but prohibited in the spiral phase. The magnetic space groups of both phases are chiral.

EuSi crystallizes in space group Cmcm (No. 63; Supplementary Tables 1–3). Single crystals were grown by the Bridgman method. Scanning transmission electron microscopy indicates high crystalline quality with few crystalline defects (Supplementary Fig. 2), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy analysis yielded an Eu:Si ratio of 50.2:49.8, consistent with stoichiometric EuSi within instrumental uncertainty (Supplementary Fig. 3). Two magnetic transitions occur at TN1 ≈ 62 K and TN2 ≈ 33.4 K, together with a weak structural distortion near the structural distortion temperature TS ≈ 60 K (Supplementary Fig. 4). Magnetization measurements along the three crystallographic axes show no pronounced hysteresis (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 6), indicating the absence of net magnetic moments at zero field. Upon cooling, these phase transitions define two boundaries: from the paramagnetic to the spiral magnetic phase, and subsequently to the conical magnetic phase (discussed later). Upon applying a magnetic field along the crystal’s a, b and c axes (Fig. 1f), the conical magnetic/spiral magnetic state exhibits metamagnetic transitions associated with spin-flop processes, and eventually evolves into a spin-polarized state at high fields (Supplementary Fig. 6c,f,i). Angular-dependent susceptibility further shows a pronounced two-fold magnetic anisotropy (Supplementary Fig. 7).

a, Temperature-dependent magnetic susceptibility measured along the a, b and c axes under zero-field-cooled (ZFC) and field-cooled (FC) conditions, respectively. The magnetic transitions at TN1 = 62 K and TN2 = 33.4 K, and structural distortion at TS = 59.7 K, are labelled. b, Magnetization versus magnetic field along the three crystallographic axes at 2 K and 40 K. The inset magnifies the low-field region, showing no distinct hysteresis. c, Resistivity of crystal S1 with current along a. The residual resistivity ratio, RRR = ρxx(300 K)/ρxx(2 K), is approximately 262. d,e, Neutron-diffraction patterns in the (H, K, 1) plane at 40 K (d) and 6 K (e). f, Temperature evolution of the (0, 4, 0) and adjacent k1 satellite peaks between 5 K and 70 K. g,h, Refined spiral and conical magnetic structures at 40 K (g) and 6 K (h). The reference Eu moment in the a–c plane is aligned along a. This convention differs from Fig. 1 by a global rotation within the a–c plane, preserving the relative moment configuration and magnetic symmetry. i, Temperature-dependent intensities of representative k1 and k2 peaks, (0, 5/3, 1) and (0, 2, 1). The dashed lines mark the magnetic transitions. CM, conical magnetic; SM, spiral magnetic; PM, paramagnetic. f.u., formula unit; r.u.l., reciprocal lattice units; Q, scattering vector; j, electrical current density.

The longitudinal resistivity is metallic, with a residual resistivity ratio (RRR = ρxx(300 K)/ρxx(2 K) ≈ 262), where ρxx is the longitudinal electrical resistivity (Fig. 2c). A sharp resistivity change near TN1 and pronounced transport anisotropy accompany the magnetic transitions (Supplementary Fig. 8). Magnetotransport measurements further reveal a large, non-saturating magnetoresistance at low temperature (reaching 4,600% at 2 K with a 9 T magnetic field along b) (Supplementary Figs. 9–12). With increasing temperature towards the spiral magnetic state, the magnetoresistance becomes negative and remains so up to room temperature, indicating strong magnetic scattering in both the spiral magnetic and paramagnetic states.

To determine the magnetic structures, we performed single-crystal neutron diffraction (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Note 5). At 40 K, satellite peaks appear at (H, K, L) ± (0, 1/3, 0) (Fig. 2d), corresponding to a magnetic propagation vector k1 = (0, 1/3, 0). Magnetic-structure refinement identifies an spiral magnetic order with moments rotating in the a–c (010) plane (Fig. 2g). The spins are approximately ferromagnetically aligned within each double layer and rotate by π/3 between adjacent double layers, corresponding to a threefold magnetic periodicity along b. This commensurate coplanar spiral is consistent with the symmetry requirements for the p-wave magnetic state discussed above.

On cooling to 6 K, the k1 satellite peaks remain, while additional magnetic intensity develops at the structural Bragg positions, corresponding to a second magnetic propagation vector k2 = (0, 0, 0) (Fig. 2e). Refinement shows that this component corresponds to a ferromagnetic moment along b, yielding the conical magnetic structure shown in Fig. 2h. The persistence of the k1 intensity across TN2 supports the coexistence of the spiral and b-axis components within the conical magnetic phase rather than macroscopic phase separation. The refined ordered moments are mac = 4.4(1) μB per Eu at 40 K and mac = 5.4(1) μB per Eu, mb = 4.1(1) μB per Eu at 6 K, where μB is the Bohr magneton, consistent with the Eu2+ valence inferred from X-ray absorption and X-ray magnetic circular dichroism measurements (Supplementary Fig. 14).

The temperature dependence of representative magnetic peaks further resolves the two transitions (Fig. 2f,i). The k1 order develops below TN1, whereas the k2 component appears below TN2. Critical exponent fits yield β = 0.32(2) for k1 and β = 0.33(3) for k2, slightly below the classical three-dimensional Heisenberg value (β = 0.365), possibly reflecting additional spin–lattice coupling.

Before turning to the spin-resolved measurements relevant for p-wave magnetism, we first characterize the overall electronic structure of EuSi across the magnetic transitions (Fig. 3). The calculated three-dimensional Fermi surface in the spiral magnetic phase (Fig. 3b) contains several electron/hole pockets exhibiting strong anisotropy along the kx, ky and kz directions. Figure 3c shows the measured band structure in the kx–kz plane, corresponding to the cleaved a–c (010) plane in the conical magnetic phase. The constant-energy contours (Fig. 3c) show clear C2 symmetry and are broadly consistent with the calculated Fermi surface; similar dispersions are observed in the conical magnetic and spiral magnetic phases.

a, Crystal and magnetic Brillouin zones (BZs) of EuSi, with the projected surface BZ of the a–c (010) cleavage plane shaded above. High-symmetry points are labelled. b, Calculated three-dimensional Fermi surface in the magnetic BZ in the spiral magnetic phase. c, Constant-energy contours at EF (i), EF − 0.1 eV (ii) and EF  − 0.2 eV (iii) in the kx–kz plane measured at 10 K. d,e, ARPES dispersion along the \(\overline{{\rm{Z}}}-\overline{\Gamma }-\overline{{\rm{X}}}\) direction, measured at 57 eV (ky ≈ 2π/b; d) and corresponding calculated bands (ky ≈ 2π/b; e). Here, b is the crystal lattice constant. f,g, ARPES dispersions measured with 7 eV photons (ky ≈ 2π/b; f) and corresponding DFT calculations at ky ≈ 2π/b (g) in the conical magnetic (i), spiral magnetic (ii) and paramagnetic (iii) phases. The α, β and γ bands are labelled. h, Temperature-dependent energy-distribution curves integrated near \(\overline{\Gamma }\) over the shaded region in f(i). Fitting resolves the peaks associated with α, β and γ. i, Temperature-dependent peak energies obtained from the energy-distribution curve fits. j, Corresponding energy separations between α and γ, β and γ, and α and β. Error bars in i represent energy uncertainties estimated from the energy resolution of the 7-eV laser-ARPES set-up at each temperature; those in j represent the corresponding propagated uncertainties in the energy separations.

The measured dispersion along the corresponding high-symmetry direction exhibits dispersive Eu 5d bands crossing EF (Fig. 3d). The measurement geometry, orbital-character analysis and determination of the high-symmetry points for the a–c cleavage plane are described in Supplementary Figs. 15 and 16. The bands near the \(\overline{\Gamma }\) point are labelled α, β and γ, and the band near the zone boundary is denoted φ, following comparison with the density functional theory (DFT) calculations in Fig. 3e. Differences in the number and precise positions of the calculated and measured bands may arise from the simplified treatment of magnetic structure, calculation parameters such as effective on-site Coulomb interaction U and lattice constant, and many-body effects (Supplementary Note 10).

Over a wider energy range, ARPES reveals the Eu 4f- and Si 3p-derived states (Supplementary Fig. 17). The Eu 4f flat bands, labelled FB1–FB3, lie approximately 1–2 eV below EF and are further identified by resonant ARPES measurements (Supplementary Fig. 18). These states are crossed by dispersive Si 3p bands, consistent with orbital-projected calculations. Their location well below EF is consistent with the localized 4f 7 configuration and large local Eu2+ moment.

The magnetic transitions are accompanied by a pronounced reconstruction of the near-EF electronic structure. High-resolution laser-ARPES demonstrates that the α, β and γ bands evolve strongly across the conical magnetic, spiral magnetic and paramagnetic phases (Fig. 3f). Their characteristic energies shift by approximately 50 meV between the conical magnetic and spiral magnetic phases, followed by a more pronounced reconstruction at TN1, where the three bands merge upon entering the paramagnetic phase (Supplementary Fig. 19). Tracking their energy positions from energy-distribution curve fits (Fig. 3h–j) shows that this reconstruction follows the temperature evolution of the in-plane magnetic order k1 determined by neutron diffraction (Fig. 2i). The calculations (Fig. 3g) reproduce the main evolution in the spiral magnetic and paramagnetic phases, whereas larger deviations occur in the conical magnetic phase, suggesting that the additional b-axis ferromagnetic component has a comparatively smaller influence on the near-EF electronic structure. Similar evolution of the α, β, γ and φ bands is observed at different photon energies and momentum directions (Supplementary Figs. 20 and 21), indicating a robust magnetism-driven reconstruction of the Eu 5d electronic structure.

We attribute this reconstruction to the strong 5d–4f exchange coupling between the localized Eu 4f moments and itinerant Eu 5d electrons through intra-atomic exchange19,20. This exchange lifts the spin degeneracy and accounts for the large band splitting with a gap of approximately 100 meV (ref. 21). Once the spiral magnetic/conical magnetic order develops, the enlarged magnetic unit cell also imposes a periodic exchange potential that folds the reconstructed 5d bands. This interpretation is consistent with the observed substantial Eu moment22. The Si p bands also show reconstruction across TN1, whereas the Eu 4f bands remain nearly unchanged in energy, although the intensity of FB1 starts to decrease at TN2 (Supplementary Fig. 22).

The dominant effect of the a–c-plane magnetic moments is further reflected in the reconstructed electronic structure across multiple momentum planes, arising from the combined effects of exchange splitting and magnetic-zone folding. Consistent reconstruction is observed by ARPES on both the cleaved b–c (100) and a–b (001) surfaces (Supplementary Note 8).

We probe the predicted p-wave symmetry using spin-resolved ARPES on the a–c cleavage plane at 40 K. The relevant symmetry relations predict opposite Sy polarization under \({k}_{y}\to -{k}_{y}\), \(E(0,{k}_{y},{k}_{z},{S}_{y})\,=\) \(E(0,-{k}_{y},{k}_{z},-{S}_{y})\) and unchanged Sy under the corresponding \({k}_{x}\to -{k}_{x}\), \(E({k}_{x},{k}_{y},{k}_{z},{S}_{y})=E(-{k}_{x},{k}_{y},{k}_{z},{S}_{y})\) operation. By varying the photon energy, we sample a series of ky values across successive magnetic Brillouin zones (Fig. 4a,b; additional measurements from an independent facility are shown in Supplementary Fig. 34). At \(({k}_{x},{k}_{y},{k}_{z})\,=\) \((0,0.3\times 2{\rm{\pi }}/b,0)\) (cut 1 in Fig. 4d; b is the magnetic-supercell lattice constant), the spectral features associated with the δ, α and γ regions show negative, positive and negative Sy polarization of approximately 5%, respectively. At the corresponding negative-ky position (cut 4 in Fig. 4d; see Supplementary Note 9 for the band assignment), the extracted polarizations show the opposite signs. For intermediate ky values approaching the nodal plane ky ≈ 0, (also −0.5 × 2π/b) the net Sy polarization is strongly suppressed (cuts 2 and 3 in Fig. 4d), consistent with the node-like behaviour expected for an odd-parity spin texture.

Cuts 1–4 (right) sample momenta along kz at different ky, accessed by varying photon energy; cuts 5 and 6 (left) compare symmetry-related momenta under \({k}_{x}\to -{k}_{x}\). Yellow and purple indicate positive and negative reduced ky, respectively, relative to each magnetic-zone centre. b, Extracted Sy polarization of spectral feature labelled α across successive magnetic Brillouin zones. The sign-changing modulation and suppression near nodal regions are consistent with the predicted p-wave spin texture. The solid curve shows calculated unfolded Sy polarization in the lattice Brillouin zone for qualitative comparison. Vertical lines mark cuts 1–4; high-symmetry points are labelled. c, Calculated Sy polarization of representative valence (val_1 and val_2) and conduction (cond_1 and cond_2) bands along ky in the magnetic Brillouin zone, shown without (top) and with (bottom) SOC. d, Spin-resolved ARPES spectra for cuts 1–4 at kx = 0. Each cut shows the spin-integrated spectrum (left), spin-resolved energy-distribution curves (right) and extracted Sy polarization (below). Dashed arrows mark the δ, α and γ spectral regions. The polarization reverses between positive and negative reduced-ky regions and is suppressed near predicted nodes (ky = 0 and −0.5  × 2π/b). b is the magnetic-supercell lattice constant. e, Spectra for cuts 5 (left) and 6 (right) at fixed ky. The extracted Sy polarization is unchanged within statistical uncertainty under \({k}_{x}\to -{k}_{x}\). Error bars in b and shaded envelopes in d and e represent one standard deviation propagated from Poisson counting statistics. These observations are consistent with the predicted spin symmetry but do not establish an eigenstate-resolved test because the measured features contain unresolved band contributions with momentum-dependent spectral weights.

To examine the momentum dependence more systematically, we extract the energy-integrated Sy polarization of the feature labelled α within the fitting-defined integration window at photon energies from 13 eV to 23 eV, sampling successive magnetic Brillouin zones. The extracted polarization exhibits a sign-changing modulation and is strongly suppressed near the ky = 0 nodal regions (Supplementary Fig. 33 and Supplementary Note 9). Despite the finite out-of-plane momentum resolution, the observed modulation is consistent with the odd-ky spin texture expected for p-wave magnetism and with the calculated spin-polarization patterns in both the lattice and magnetic Brillouin zones (Fig. 4b,c and Supplementary Figs. 35 and 36). The variation in modulation amplitude across successive zones is also consistent with momentum-dependent unfolded spectral weights, which redistribute contributions from folded magnetic-supercell states at different extended-zone momenta (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 36). The persistence of the same sign-reversal pattern in calculations with and without SOC (Fig. 4c) further indicates that the dominant spin texture originates from magnetic symmetry rather than SOC.

In addition, we find that the Sy polarization of the spectral features associated with the δ, α and γ regions remains unchanged within statistical uncertainty for symmetry-related points (kx, ky) and (−kx, ky), consistent with \(E({k}_{x},{k}_{y},{k}_{z},{S}_{y})=E(-{k}_{x},{k}_{y},{k}_{z},{S}_{y})\) (Fig. 4e).

We note two limitations of the spin-ARPES analysis. First, the measured polarization is small, approximately 5%, compared with the calculated maximum contrast of about 25% (Fig. 4c), and the clearest spin-resolved features occur at finite binding energies within the near-EF electronic structure rather than at EF. The measured spin polarization may be reduced by finite energy and momentum resolution and by partial cancellation between unresolved contributions with opposite spin polarizations. Averaging over oppositely chiral magnetic domains could further reduce the signal if such domains are sampled within the illuminated area. Second, the near-EF features contain contributions from multiple folded bands with momentum-dependent spectral weights, and the cuts at positive and negative reduced ky were acquired using different photon energies and sample different extended-zone momenta, so the relative spectral weights contributing to a measured feature may differ. The measurements therefore do not constitute a one-to-one, eigenstate-resolved test of the calculated symmetry relations. In particular, the present data do not uniquely separate the momentum dependence of individual-band spin polarization from changes in the relative spectral weights of unresolved components. Within these limitations, the sign-changing Sy modulation and its suppression near the predicted nodal regions provide spin-resolved spectroscopic evidence consistent with the predicted odd-parity p-wave spin texture of the reconstructed near-EF electronic structure of EuSi.

The large local magnetic moment and its strong coupling with the electronic structure enable the measurement of the magnetic domains with different chiralities using complementary probes23,24. Figure 5a shows the magnetic domains on the a–c plane measured by MFM in the conical magnetic phase, revealing a bubble-in-stripe pattern with a characteristic width of approximately 10 μm, corresponding to opposite spiral configurations. Similar stripe-like magnetic domains are observed by circularly polarized micro-ARPES with a submicrometre beam spot (Fig. 5b).

The lift height is 200 nm and the colour scale is 5 Hz. b, Micro-ARPES domain map of the same crystallographic plane at 20 K using circularly right-polarized (CR) light. c, Left: composite band spectra from domains A (point 1) and B (point 3), marked in b, measured with CR light. IA and IB denote the photoemission intensities from domains A and B, respectively, displayed in blue and red channels.
