#1256. Pedro Neto is sent off for two yellow cards in under two minutes before bizarre touchline clash with Craig Bellamy - as Portugal beat Wales with Bruno Fernandes on target

Published: 17:34 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 17:49 EST, 17 November 2026

Chelsea star Pedro Neto lost his cool while playing for Portugal in their win over Wales as he received two yellow cards in as many minutes before clashing with opposing manager Craig Bellamy.

The Blues winger had in fact scored in the game, netting his side's second goal at the Cardiff City Stadium, but saw his game fall apart in the second-half.

He was first booked for a high challenge on the back of Brennan Johnson's leg – a tackle which some may argue could have been a red in itself.

One minute and 59 seconds later, he was shown his second yellow when he slid in on Johnson again. He didn't appear to make too much contact, if any, but left the Wales man sprawling to avoid it.

German referee Sven Jablonski showed no hesitation in sending Neto off, but the winger wasn't going to take it lying down.

He had to be held back by captain Bruno Fernandes as he tried to confront Johnson, and seemingly managed to shout in his direction before reluctantly making his way off the field.

Pedro Neto was sent off while playing for Portugal against Wales after two yellow cards in under two minutes

He also had a confrontation with Wales manager Craig Bellamy (right) as he left the field of play

Before that, though, he had a conversation with Wales boss Craig Bellamy, with officials initially trying to separate the two, with Neto looking angry.

Bellamy, though, spoke to Neto and embraced him before finally walking down the tunnel.

The 26-year-old will now serve a one-game suspension, meaning he will miss the first leg of Portugal's Nations League quarter-final, which will be played in March.

Jorge Jesus's side secured top spot in their group with the win over Wales, which was achieved by Carlos Forbs's 70th-minute goal.

Fernandes had opened the scoring for his side in the 11th minute, but David Brooks and Sorba Thomas gave Wales an unlikely lead.

That was until Neto levelled things up just before half-time, and Forbs scored the winner, with ten-man Portugal able to hold on for all three points.

Wales finished bottom of the group with one win – against Norway – and five defeats from their six matches.

Captain Ben Davies said after the game: 'We showed a lot of character and we've shown good effort in these games where we've just come up short from a results perspective.

After expressing his frustration, the Chelsea star had to be directed off the field by captain Bruno Fernandes (right)

He had in fact scored for his side in the game, bringing them level before the half-time interval

'There is a lot to take from this going into the games in March and we have to feel confident because we've been playing well.

'We know the boys up top can be so dangerous, and if teams want to come here and play man-for-man against us, we've got a lot of speed and we have to be good on the ball. That comes with risk sometimes, like you saw with the chances that they had, but I'd rather play this way and go toe-to-toe with these teams and have a go.

'We competed in the campaign and we were not a million miles off like the table might suggest. I thought we put in some very good performances, we just wished we had some better results.'

Neto, meanwhile, will now return to his club side Chelsea ahead of a busy Christmas period.

He has started all but one Premier League game so far and has been a key player under new manager Xabi Alonso.

The Blues will take on Leeds at Stamford Bridge this weekend as club football returns.

#1255. Liverpool’s £400m front line clicks but win at Brentford turns on red card

Only time will tell if Liverpool’s £400m front line can ever justify the extraordinary amount of money that was spent on them, but this was at least a significant step in the right direction. In a gritty victory away to Brentford, all four of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Victor Muñoz either scored or assisted goals.

Admittedly, the task was made significantly easier by the major turning point of this game: a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk. At the time of Yarmoliuk’s “headbutting action” towards Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet, the visitors were trailing 1-0 and looking worryingly short of ideas in attack.

But as the context of the match changed, so did the level of threat from the visitors. Against 10 men, with more space in which to operate, Liverpool’s forwards looked increasingly dangerous. Wirtz began to pull the strings, Barcola started to cause problems, Muñoz stretched the Brentford defence and Isak became a lurking menace.

For Andoni Iraola, who had failed to beat Brentford in six attempts as manager of Bournemouth, it would have made for an immensely pleasing sight. After last weekend’s thrashing by Manchester City, Liverpool have responded with a 6-3 Champions League win over LASK and this victory against a previously unbeaten Brentford. Iraola will know, however, that his team’s numerical advantage was the fundamental reason for the dramatic shift in the flow of this game.

The Gtech Community Stadium simmered with outrage following Yarmoliuk’s red card, which came in the eighth minute of first-half stoppage time, and the home fans probably had a point. Yes, there was a movement of the midfielder’s head towards Jacquet, but it was hardly an act of violence. Jacquet’s reaction, collapsing to the turf in mock agony, was embarrassing but predictably effective. Cynics would say the Frenchman changed the game for his team. Purists would argue this is no way in which to influence a match.

Keith Andrews, the Brentford head coach, chose against complaining too aggressively. But he did make it clear what he thought of Jacquet’s behaviour. “I do think they were cute and clever,” Andrews said. “He is walking into Yarmo. But we need to look at ourselves and I understand why it was a red. Yarmo is an amazing young man and he will learn from this.”

Brentford had been the better team before this decisive incident and they deserved their lead, given to them by a majestic header by Keane Lewis-Potter, from Igor Thiago’s cross. It was a moment of attacking quality that Iraola’s glitzy attackers had looked unlikely to replicate, especially when Barcola fluffed a one-versus-one showdown with Brentford goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher.

To play an entire half of Premier League football with only 10 men is a brutal examination, though, and Brentford were unable to pass the test. Wirtz unleashed Muñoz after an hour, allowing the Spaniard to fire home with his left foot, before Barcola’s header found Isak in the box with 20 minutes remaining.

It was Isak’s fifth goal of the campaign, which means he has now beaten last season’s tally of four. He has scored in all five of his Premier League appearances against Brentford. “I didn’t have too many chances,” Isak said. “I was waiting for my moment.”

Any hopes of a Brentford comeback evaporated in stoppage time, when the home side lost another man to a red card. This time it was Vitaly Janelt, who received his second yellow for fouling Rio Ngumoha, Liverpool’s sparkling teenage winger. From there, Liverpool’s attempts to score a third were comically poor. “We lacked some composure,” admitted Iraola. “But it was a good battle today, and very important points for us. To take three points here is very valuable.”

An encouraging result for Liverpool, then, but this was not an afternoon without concerns. The first-half showing was worrying, and there were also injuries to Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong. Both players limped off, and Iraola said they will now be out “for some time”.

The loss of Szoboszlai will be a particular concern, as he was rushed back from a hamstring injury for this game but then felt the same muscle again after only 32 minutes of action. “It’s a very delicate situation,” said Iraola.

The injury to Frimpong meant that Muñoz, a winger, played most of the second half as an attack-minded right-back. He did so excellently, and took his goal with impressive composure after Wirtz had pushed the ball into his path. Liverpool’s second was similarly clinical, as Isak pounced on Barcola’s knock-down in a congested penalty area. These, clearly, are the moments of game-changing quality that Liverpool expect from their big-money forwards. Iraola will hope it was a sign of things to come.

Speaking to Sky Sports after his first Premier League win as Fulham head coach, Arbeloa said: “I’m so happy, happy for my players, happy for my supporters, happy for everyone at the club that they deserve this victory. We [waited] a lot of time and some many games that I think we deserved this victory before, but today we did a very good game and yes, I can’t believe that the game finished just 1-0.”

9 - Florian Wirtz's nine chances created from open play against Brentford is the most by a player in a Premier League game since Sadio Mané v Burnley in January 2021 (9) and the most by a player in an away game since Samir Nasri v Spurs in August 2011 (10). Progress. https://t.co/xyMIQP9y5p

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the 3pm kick-offs. Manchester City burst the Anfield bubble last weekend but were defeated by Paris St-Germain in a Champions League thriller on Wednesday, and Enzo Maresca will have to manage his leading cast members’ workload. Before Ipswich Town’s visit to the Etihad he floated the idea of resting some of his players at some point.

“We are thinking about this not just with Erling [Haaland] because we have players, unfortunately or fortunately, they are playing all the games with us and all the games with the international teams,” Maresca said in his pre-match press conference.”

“Elliot [Anderson], Enzo [Fernández], Marc [Guéhi], Erling, Rúben [Dias] – so at some point we probably need to give them some rest.”

Ipswich’s spirited start to the season was characterised by a stunning late turnaround against Fulham last weekend. Gary O’Neil’s side have accrued three wins in their first six top-flight matches for the first time since 1993 and may consider today’s match as something of a free hit.

Elsewhere, Liverpool’s confidence-building midweek win in Austria was underlined by Bradley Barcola’s first, second and third goals for the club. It was exactly what the France winger needed, and with Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo emerging as doubts for this afternoon’s trip to Brentford, the attacking burden may fall on Barcola and Florian Wirtz’s shoulders once more.

Breaking down fourth-placed Brentford, who are one of only three teams to remain undefeated this season, will be a tall task. Keith Andrews’ stock has never been higher, but the same cannot be said for Álvaro Arbeloa, whose winless Fulham are bottom of the league.

Pressure was already mounting before Fulham’s three-game run against the promoted teams, and the late collapse at Portman Road will not have helped the Spaniard’s cause. Defeat by Hull City will not be seen kindly by the club’s hierarchy.

#1252. 'We felt like medieval peasants coming up against a king': Insiders relive the battle to rid Blackpool of the Oystons, from tangerines stuffed in knickers to a bright orange GTI - and why 'insider dealing' claims mean club isn't out of the woods yet

Published: 07:55 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 18:12 EST, 17 November 2026

In the south London pub where they are readying themselves for a League One match with AFC Wimbledon, Blackpool fans who fought for their club’s heart and soul, 10 years ago, receive a message informing them that half the squad have gone down with a sickness bug so severe that the starting XI will be very unusual.

Three players are too ill to leave the team hotel, the goalkeeper selected is yet to feature in the league this season and the EFL don’t consider this predicament serious enough to cancel the game. The club are already on a run of five defeats in seven.

Moments like this reveal the Blackpool fanbase’s deep sense of perspective, born of their long and often wretched fight to kick out one of British football’s most detested owners, Owen Oyston.

‘We’re still here and we’re watching our club home and away,’ says Andy Higgins, chair of the Blackpool Supporters Trust. ‘We have a good relationship with the club,’ says his friend Dave Ragozzino, with Higgins in the Earlsfield pub. ‘The club are asking us to tell fans what’s going on, and they know we will help. Ten years ago, our club’s owners were suing us.’

The story of the campaign which brought these fans and many more together is told in a superb new documentary The Battle for Blackpool, which screens this week, capturing its spirit, imagination and intelligence.

Oyston and his son Karl have both cooperated with the documentary-makers. Oyston Snr, wearing dark shades and his trademark fedora, is interviewed at his stately home in the Forest of Bowland, while his son Karl, clearly still consumed with hate and contempt for fans, is filmed clay pigeon shooting across their estate.

Blackpool fans watch their team fall to another League One defeat, at AFC Wimbledon on Saturday

The Tangerines are just two points above the relegation zone having lost five out of their last seven league fixtures

Their supporters fought a long and wretched battle against the club's former owner Owen Oyston (pictured in 2017)

The film’s stars are the supporters who led the fight – Christine Seddon, Tim Fielding, Ragozzino, two fans in a Mk1 tangerine Golf GTI and twin sisters of advancing years who embraced the campaign’s guerilla tactics.

Oyston Jr, who chaired the club at his mother’s request after his father was jailed for rape in 1996, tells the documentary-makers: ‘My father likes football. I didn’t.’

It was after he’d stumbled on a managerial genius in Ian Holloway, who took the club into the Premier League for a season in 2010-11, that a full sense of the family’s greed and entitlement became clear.

The Mail on Sunday's Nick Harris revealed that Oyston Snr had paid himself £11million out of the Premier League jackpot, while critics say virtually all the club appeared to get out of promotion was a new sprinkler system. The fight against the Oystons took hold. The Blackpool Supporters Trust, then chaired by Fielding, was its strategic and political wing, flanked by the imaginative sabotage activities of the Tangerine Knights group.

A plot to smuggle tennis balls into the ground for a home match against Burnley, in April 2014, and collectively throw them on the pitch, provides one of the documentary’s many glorious sections. Fans stuffed the missiles into their pants, socks and bras.

‘I had them in my knickers,’ says Christine Atkinson, who is interviewed with her twin sister, Pauline O’Rourke. ‘I didn’t have tennis balls. I had tangerines. It was softer. Less uncomfortable!’

The family of Karl Oyston mocked the tennis ball protest on social media. But it was when his father began suing ordinary fans, some pensioners, for criticising him that the protest escalated.

‘My father created a whole department, scouring message boards full-time so he could sue them,’ Oyston Jr tells the film-makers.

‘I had tangerines in my knickers,’ says Pauline O'Rourke (right), who is interviewed with her twin sister, Christine Atkinson, in the documentary about Blackpool's fight to get rid of the owners

‘My father created a whole department, scouring message boards full-time so he could sue them,’ Oyston Jr (pictured in 2010) tells the film-makers

‘We felt like medieval peasants, coming up against a king,’ says Tangerine Knight Kevin Quirke, interviewed with his fellow combatant Scott Koudellas inside the tangerine GTI, parked up on Blackpool’s South Shore – one of the film’s many wonderful touches.

Ragozzino lost his job and faced a £150,000 legal suit. Fielding, a solicitor, was told it would cost more than £250,000 to defend himself against Oyston’s legal action. The Oystons forced him to pay them £10,000 in cash and issue a public apology.

Karl Oyston reveals how much he revelled in the war with fans, delighting in the ‘Oyston Out’ personalised number plate his wife bought for Christmas to maintain the mockery. ‘She thought it was highly amusing. Which it was,’ he relates.

Suing elderly Blackpool fans was his father’s idea, he says. ‘But as soon as the board makes a decision, you fight to the death to support it.’

Oyston Snr maintains he was perfectly entitled to pay himself £11m of the Premier League money. ‘Why wouldn’t we? Why shouldn’t we?’ he asks. ‘We own the company. We’d had 25 years of pouring money down the drain without the least prospect of seeing any of it ever again.’

It was Fielding who came up with the game-changing strategy – persuading minority shareholder Valeri Belokon to mount a successful legal challenge against the Oystons, eventually clearing the way for Simon Sadler, a Hong Kong-based financier and Blackpudlian to buy the club.

It’s not been a bed of roses these past few years. An interim club board, formed after Oyston was ousted, included Ben Hatton, later chief operating officer at Aston Villa, former Inter Milan CEO Mike Bolingbroke and Fielding. But a succession of good leaders have left.

Brett Gerrity, a one-time close friend of Sadler who persuaded him to buy the club, resigned in 2023. The two no longer get on. Ben Mansford, respected ex-CEO at Leeds and Barnsley, also unexpectedly left. Former sporting director David Downes was recently made CEO. Amid these comings and goings, Sadler has not appointed a successful manager since Neil Critchley left to assist Steven Gerrard at Aston Villa in 2022.

‘We felt like medieval peasants, coming up against a king,’ says Tangerine Knight Kevin Quirke (right), interviewed with his fellow combatant Scott Coudellas inside the tangerine GTI

Christine Seddon was a leading figure in the fight to rid Blackpool of the Oystons

None of this has affected fans’ views of Sadler, a boyhood Blackpool fan whose investment is still giving the club a top eight budget in League One. He has spent money on upgrades to the stadium and training ground and the team’s playing surface is excellent.

But his own future at Bloomfield Road is in doubt. He is on trial in Hong Kong over accusations of insider dealing linked to his former hedge fund and could face a prison sentence if convicted.

That would mean him failing the EFL Owners’ and Directors’ Test and he would seemingly have to sell. The verdict in that case is expected next February. Sadler, who has pleaded not guilty to the charges, has revealed little of any contingencies he might have made. He is thought to be prepared to sell the club, though only if the buyer will be a true custodian.

‘He’s acutely aware of not putting Blackpool right back where it was with Oyston,’ says one source.

‘The club is so much better and professional than it used to be,' Seddon tells us. ‘But we are short of football business experience. We don’t have a proper board at the moment.

'Hedge fund management – our owner’s world – does not always translate well into football. It’s a steep learning curve.’

Oyston Snr revealed in a recent interview that he wants to buy the club back and gift a majority share to fans. ‘In 2015, we suggested to him that he walk away and leave the club’s assets to the fans,’ says Seddon.

‘He ignored us, yet now he’s suggesting this. These are deluded ramblings. Simon Sadler would not give Oyston the time of day.’

'When I hear some fans complaining about the club, I think: “Have you forgotten? Are your memories quite short?”'

Karl Oyston tells the documentary-makers that he has not spoken to his 92-year-old father since the family’s 32-year ownership of the club ended in 2019. Will he ever see him again, he is asked. ‘No. That ship’s sailed,’ he replies.

Blackpool, backed by a loud, strong away following, fell to a 1-0 defeat at Wimbledon and boss Ian Evatt’s job will be on the line when they face fellow-strugglers Wigan on Saturday, so the film is a particularly timely reminder of how far this club’s fans have come.

‘Yes, we want results to be better,’ Seddon says. ‘But when I hear some complaining about the club, I think: “Have you forgotten? Are your memories quite short?” Our club became an opportunity for people who were dismantling it for their own benefit. There were times when we thought we would lose it altogether.

'But we’re now in a place where we were beginning to believe we would never be. We’re thankful for that.’

The Battle for Blackpool will premiere in the UK on November 21 on Sky Documentaries and streaming service NOW

#1251. Bundesliga treat Harry Kane's Ballon d'Or as beacon of hope as Germany's competitiveness questions linger

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Even if the hints of a smile never fully leave his face, there is an overriding sense of practicality when Philipp Lahm speaks. He seems to have shed the intensity associated with the life of a professional athlete nearly a decade after retiring, but the characteristics of a World Cup-winning captain are hard to miss. He is friendly and open but also serious, so when the topic of conversation shifts to Harry Kane's Ballon d'Or triumph, he is politely unflinching in his assessment of what the award means for soccer in Germany.

"It helped Harry Kane and Michael Olise that they came from another country," Lahm said four days after Kane's big win. "I think it's quite difficult for a German player playing in the Bundesliga [to win the Ballon d'Or]."

A quick glance at the data would confirm the hypothesis. The last Bundesliga-based player and the last German player to win the sport's most prestigious individual award was Borussia Dortmund's Matthias Sammer in 1996. A German player has only finished inside the top three of the Ballon d'Or three times since, the last being Manuel Neuer in 2014, while Kane is only the seventh Bundesliga player to rank in the top three since Sammer's win. Lahm seamlessly links the pattern to another less-than-ideal trend in Germany's top flight -- Bayern Munich, with whom he won eight Bundesliga titles, are the division's indisputable kings.

They have lost the title just once since the 2012-13 season, a lack of competitiveness at the top of the table a natural consequence of their dominance. This is, in some ways, not Bayern's problem, but a narrative persists in Germany regardless. Players have historically been unable to reach the peaks of the game in Germany because of the circumstances, inspiring a wide-ranging set of side effects. Kane's move to Bayern was not designed to be anything other than the right move at the right time for a player talented enough to compete for the UEFA Champions League, but three years later, those invested in the Bundesliga's success are beginning to treat him as a beacon of hope.

"I do hope that the good players stay in the Bundesliga," Lahm said, "so I'm hopeful through Harry Kane that a lot of other players will follow because it's possible to win and play here."

The argument to join Bayern Munich is a straightforward one, if you ask sporting director Christoph Freund -- "you can win titles with us," both in Germany and Europe. Bayern have won the Champions League twice in the last 14 years, a feat matched only by Paris Saint-Germain and topped by Real Madrid. The Bundesliga's distribution of wealth favors them in this case, to the point that it likely played a sizable role in signing Kane and Olise. The balance of financial power in the European club game, though, has shifted as Bayern re-established their foothold in Germany -- the Premier League has become the sport's league of choice because it has the financial might to back up the claim. Players like Robert Lewandowski and Mario Gotze used to prove their worth at other German clubs (and in their specific case, Borussia Dortmund) before climbing up the food chain and joining Bayern. Florian Wirtz's jump from Bayer Leverkusen to Liverpool in 2025, though, is an example of a new world order, one some hope Kane's Ballon d'Or might change.

"It's all about the attention, so when you're successful with the German national team that's visible, but then when you play also successful soccer with Liverpool, then the attention in U.K. is much bigger," Lahm said, citing Wirtz's hypothetical Ballon d'Or case as an example, "so that would be more difficult for a German player in the Bundesliga alone, rather than changing to somewhere else outside and being successful abroad."

The Bundesliga's international appeal has not only taken a hit on the sporting side in recent years. Bayern's executives believe their club makes up around 50% of the league's brand value globally, and though they are unapologetic about their strengths on the pitch, they also argue they are doing too much of the heavy lifting. Rouven Kasper, a member of Bayern's executive board, pointed to Premier League clubs' oversized presence on preseason tours as a primary example for the Bundesliga to follow but all but questioned the league's interest in the strategy.

"The league needs to be, as well, stronger and bring more reach, but the league exists from the clubs," Kasper said. "We are the spearhead of German football, and I think together with the other clubs and together with the league, we need to be even more active in the markets ... it's not enough, and at the end, it's about people, community. We want to be approachable. We want to talk to the people. We want to be there, as the Bundesliga and Bayern alone cannot do it together with Dortmund, so we need more activities from the league and being in different markets, as the U.K. guys are doing and also the Spanish guys are doing. We will do our part."

Their part includes potentially using Kane as a hook for player recruitment, even if other leagues have their charms for the world's top talents.

"I think everybody knows the Premier League is the biggest league at the moment," Freund said. "Also, Spain is really attractive with Real Madrid and Barcelona, but we know we are Bayern Munich and the German Bundesliga is also really a strong league, a really good league, outstanding stadiums, outstanding atmosphere, and you can [perform] also on a very high level like Harry, the next step in his career, and therefore, I think Bayern Munich and also the German Bundesliga is very attractive, also, for international top players."

Some in the Bundesliga, though, are resigned to the fact that there are certain things Bayern -- and other European clubs -- will simply beat them to. Dortmund have held strong in their attempts to mount a title challenge this season, level on points with Bayern after eight games thanks to Saturday's 2-2 draw in Der Klassiker. For the foreseeable future, though, recruitment of elite talents cannot and will not play a central role in their quest to win silverware. "We never refuse, or we never avoid to tell you guys where we are from, but in comparison to Munich, Madrid, London, Paris, Milan, we are from Dortmund and from a purely economic perspective, we are far behind them," Borussia Dortmund CEO Carsten Cramer said. "If they [are] just interested in trophies and silver, if they look for the Ballon d'Or player wearing a black and yellow shirt, maybe that is something we can't offer to them."

While Bayern's brand is wrapped in the quiet luxury of their domestic stronghold, Cramer argued that Dortmund's appeal is a qualitative one.

"In the last 13 years, we didn't become champion but though we didn't become champion, the interest in Dortmund is still increasing and the amount of people following our club on social media and wherever we travel in the world is quite huge," he said. "We are able to offer a different approach: closeness. That is the Dortmund way, and I think that is maybe one of the reasons that many, many hardcore supporters of one club do have a sympathy for us as a second-love club, which I do not complain about, and that is our way. I don't want to make us too small by saying we are a niche club, but we are for sure a bit different, and I don't complain about [it]."

Patrick Owomoyela, a defender for Jurgen Klopp's Dortmund team that won back-to-back Bundesliga titles more than a decade ago, can clearly map out the recipe to beat Bayern to the top. Strong squad composition and compatibility go a long way, and he believes the current iteration of Dortmund has that -- he praised head coach Niko Kovac's defensive structure and commended him for "sprinkling the creativity" into the team in the months since taking the job in January 2025. There is just one problem, though.

"Even though you know the recipe, the soup is not always the same," he said. "Even though you put in the same ingredients, it's not always tasting the same, and if it does, maybe it's not the perfect soup, you know? So you need to find that special something."

Much like Cramer, Owomoyela has a qualitative argument of his own to make when it comes to breaking Bayern's decades-long dominance in the Bundesliga. The "special something" for his Dortmund team was a sense of camaraderie, the foundation of which was Klopp's joyous approach, though he openly admitted that is a difficult thing to replicate.

"This is sometimes the mentality of the guys or the personality of the guys and how that fits together, on top of the stuff that they can do with the ball and as I said, we weren't the best in terms of playing football," he said. "We were the best team. We had the most fun. We really liked doing a lot of stuff together. We were like a family, and you don't find that all the time, and it gets harder, I would say, every year because football has changed. The plans of players nowadays are totally different ... These guys have a plan, so they want to be part of something for this period of time, but then they want to move on, and that makes it, of course, hard to find that chemistry because he is gone next year."

It is the issue he identified with Leverkusen, the Bundesliga's last champion not named Bayern. Their rise up the ranks in the 2023-24 season was ambitious and impressive, but two years later, the mainstays of their title-winning campaign were elsewhere. Wirtz left for Liverpool, as did Jeremie Frimpong, Granit Xhaka now finds himself at Sunderland, Piero Hincapie now plays for Arsenal and then-head coach Xabi Alonso made a stop at Real Madrid before landing at his current post at Chelsea. Jonathan Tah, meanwhile, went the old-school route and now plays at Bayern. The next challenger to Bayern's throne will likely face the same fate for the foreseeable future, no matter whether its stars move to Munich or settle in England.

Saturday's draw between Bayern and Dortmund, though, has offered a flicker of optimism that the Bundesliga might have a title race on its hands before the next great team gets stripped for parts. The 2-2 scoreline flatters Dortmund -- Bayern racked up 4.48 expected goals and were unlucky when the crossbar denied them on both Kane's second-half penalty and a late strike from Lennart Karl, while the visitors generated just 0.74 xG. Owomoyela argued, though, that Bayern have their flaws.

"What's it gonna take to take that away from Bayern after all these years again?" he asked. "It's just to believe that it's possible and I think the Bayern team showed in this season as well, or especially maybe, that you can wound them, you can hurt them and something is possible. You can see that in almost every game they played, even in that cup game [against second-division side Magdeburg on Oct. 28] that they just had and they won it 6-1 ... They hit the post, hit the crossbar, scored a goal, had two other big chances so now take a team with more quality, with the right kind of belief, there might be something possible."

Saturday's Klassiker only added to the Bundesliga's week of good news, presenting a different case of the league's strengths than Kane's Ballon d'Or triumph, one that will likely take precedence in the short term. The longer Dortmund keep pace with Bayern, the more intriguing the Bundesliga becomes, and at this stage of the season, the possibility of a genuine title race is easy enough to dream up. That sense of optimism, though, tends to give way to the league's current realities. Even if Dortmund answered the question in the affirmative once, there's a long way to go until anyone can definitively say that Bayern can be topped.

"We weren't really eye-level competitors," Owomoyela said about Dortmund's ability to compete with Bayern in the years since their back-to-back Bundesliga titles. "We were there and we were able to hunt, but from a little distance, and I think everybody understands that."

Newcastle United look like a poor team playing badly. The evidence is increasingly damning after Matthias Jaissle’s side were loudly booed off at the end of this limp defeat.

This has all the makings of a long, hard season. Anger is already rising to the surface, even though Jaissle claimed Newcastle deserved more from a game they “controlled” in the first half and “dominated” in the second. Those comments jarred with what we had just seen.

After four years of enjoying an upward trajectory under Eddie Howe, the team faded last season, sold their best players in the summer, lost the manager and there is no evidence yet they have replaced anything with better.

This was supposed to be a reaction to the embarrassing 4-1 thrashing at Coventry City, but it led to another loss and, in the first half at least, another abject display. Aston Villa were always the more fluent and more threatening. They should have won by more than just Johan Manzambi’s first-half header.

Johan Manzambi heads Aston Villa in front! 🟣 https://t.co/jxZf2568Sl

It is getting hard to comprehend what Jaissle wants his team to do. The much-hyped “vertical” style looks like an ugly incarnation of the long ball football of yesteryear. They did not like it at Newcastle in the 1980s and 1990s and some fashions should never return. It is in danger of resembling a shell suit that has emerged from the back of the wardrobe for a Saturday night out.

There is so much confidence in the German in the Newcastle boardroom that they believe improvement is inevitable, but that is far from assured. Newcastle are not getting better; they are making all the same mistakes and, if anything, as an attacking force, they are looking increasingly stale and predictable. #1247. How Mauricio Pochettino's culture shock tactics will resurrect Man United: From 'Murderball' training that leaves players throwing up to telling Harry Kane to slim down and why even the smell of the kit must be spot on

Published: 21:00 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 17 November 2026

When the entertaining but ultimately rather pointless Ralf Rangnick was tasked with holding the fort as manager at Manchester United five years ago, he was asked whether his much-admired style of football – the high-intensity gegenpress aped by disciples such as Jurgen Klopp – could work with a team that had Cristiano Ronaldo, 36, and Edinson Cavani, 34, in it.

Rangnick replied that he was certain it could. The German was, of course, proved very wrong.

It is this kind of strange, blinkered hubris that we should not expect Mauricio Pochettino to bring with him to Old Trafford.

Heaven knows we have seen enough of that in recent times. Ruben Amorim and his back three. Erik ten Hag and… well maybe one day we will understand what all that was supposed to be about.

But no, this will not be Pochettino. This cannot be Pochettino.

This United squad is not one built for the new United manager’s favoured kind of front-foot, hurrying and harrying football. This is not Tottenham Hotspur 2016. It is not Kyle Walker, Toby Alderweireld, Son Heung-min and Harry Kane. It is not physical and youthful and energetic.

Mauricio Pochettino is waving goodbye to the US national team and hello to Man United this week. But he faces a daunting task at Old Trafford

This United squad is not one built for the new United manager’s favoured kind of front-foot, hurrying and harrying football

That is why Pochettino’s battle – at least for the remainder of this season – will be about hearts and minds as much as it is about anything revolutionary that he can bring to bear on the training fields of Carrington.

The good news for those hoping for quick improvement is that Pochettino – at least the one who took Spurs to a Champions League final in 2019 and to within a sniff of a Premier League title a few years earlier – is adept at the mental and emotional side of football. It is upon this that, initially at least, he may wish to rely.

Son told me about this when we sat down to look back on his career in England. He was prolific under Pochettino, a scorer of 75 goals in four-and-a-half seasons under the Argentine. But it was not always like that. Once – just like several current players at United – he was disaffected and unhappy.

‘Mauricio turned me round and it wasn’t about football,’ Son told me. ‘It was about me as a person and how he made he feel.

‘I needed help, basically. And he gave me it.

'He did so many good things that I can't even say the words. It was unbelievable.

‘Sometimes he had been my coach and sometimes he had been like my family.’

Pochettino inherits a jigsaw puzzle with the wrong-shaped pieces at Old Trafford. It’s a squad put together for and by six different managers.

Pochettino will want to improve the fitness levels at United and his intense methods might feel like an ice bath to their players

'He did so many good things that I can't even say the words,' says Son Heung-min of his manager at Tottenham. 'It was unbelievable... sometimes he was like my family’

On arrival this week, for example, he will renew acquaintances with Luke Shaw, one of his old Southampton players signed for Louis van Gaal at United back in 2014. Shaw – the club’s only real left back – is 31 now and recovering from injury.

The physical limitations of this United team were clear in the titanic but ultimately rather pitiful 4-4 draw with Aston Villa that proved to be Michael Carrick’s last game in charge just before the international break.

Invited back into a game they trailed 2-0, United’s front four briefly chased the life out of Villa when Unai Emery’s team were in possession. For 20 minutes, Villa could not get out of their own half.

But the likes of Bruno Fernandes, Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo and Amad Diallo simply could not maintain that level of exertion once the surge in adrenaline had spiked. By the time the game reached the hour mark, United were 4-2 down.

It is certain Pochettino will wish to improve some levels of fitness at United and his methods will perhaps feel like an ice bath to some of those United players who have approached the basic prerequisite of running like some kind of optional extra at times this season.

At Spurs, players were occasionally known to vomit during training. Pochettino told Harry Kane he could be the best striker in the world but not until he lost weight.

Six or seven years later at Chelsea, meanwhile, he punished striker Nicolas Jackson for picking up five largely needless yellow cards by ordering him to run laps of the training pitch. Jackson was only told why it was happening as he lay on the grass in a heap afterwards.

Pochettino took many of his principles from his compatriot and former manager Marcelo Bielsa whose ‘Murderball’ sessions eventually arrived in England during his spell at Leeds United eight years ago. The stated aim is simple.

The likes of Bruno Fernandes (centre) have struggled to maintain the physicality Pochettino will demand across 90 minutes in games this season

Pochettino took many of his principles from his compatriot and former manager Marcelo Bielsa

‘With Mauricio, there is no hiding,’ said former Southampton midfielder Adam Lallana on the Rest Is Football podcast.

‘Everything is high-intensity, pressing from the front, and repeating sprints again and again in training so that it becomes automatic on a Saturday.’

Trawl through Pochettino’s time as a frontline coach and the testimonies of unstinting, high-intensity work are strikingly similar. There has been no great change in the belief, even when he arrived in America to coach the US national team ahead of this summer’s World Cup.

'He brings that club intensity into the national team environment,’ says Juventus midfielder Weston McKennie. ‘You immediately feel the tempo he expects.’

For this to work well, a coach needs two things. A pre-season in which to embed that specific kind of fitness and a squad assembled to play that way.

At United, Pochettino has neither so we can expect it to be a slow burn. He is approaching the busiest period of the playing schedule – his team will play 12 games in the next six and a half weeks – and has immobile central defenders, full backs with limitations and a midfield unit that lacks legs when compared to the best in the Premier League and Europe.

Equally, Pochettino arrives back in a Premier League where many teams now trade off the same high-press principles that were once rather new. Ten years ago, it was Klopp’s Liverpool. Now it’s Fabian Hurzeler’s Brighton and many, many others.

Every player has a brain and a mind, though, and it is here that Pochettino will in all likelihood seek to make the greatest gains ahead of Sunday’s trip to Liverpool and beyond.

Pochettino arrives back in a Premier League where many teams now trade off the same high-press principles that were once rather new when he landed at Southampton in 2013

Pochettino can be blunt with players. He told Harry Kane he could be the best striker in the world but not until he lost weight

There is not a United manager since the end of the Sir Alex Ferguson era who has not run into trouble with individual players at some point. Ten Hag with Ronaldo, Jadon Sancho and Raphael Varane. Amorim with Marcus Rashford and Kobbie Mainoo. Carrick with his captain, Fernandes.

This, as much as anything, is what has held United back this season. United do not have a squad fit to win the league but that it sits in the bottom three says everything for the way Carrick and his coaching staff failed at their side of the deal.

Pochettino’s friendship with Ferguson is more than a decade old and endures. Ferguson will be thrilled at the appointment. Indeed, there are similarities to be found between the two. Pochettino, for example, is a small details man, a coach who understands that mood and motivation and cohesion can be just as important as tactics or indeed anything the opposition can bring on a Saturday afternoon.

Having reached out yesterday to a former Southampton player for input on his ex-manager’s methods, the former international gave an insight – albeit unwittingly – into the kind of loyalty Pochettino can inspire.

‘We need to let him integrate at United his own way,’ came the reply. ‘I don’t think he needs us talking about his secrets.’

Pochettino can be blunt with players. He was with Son. He was with Kane.

‘He said, “You need to do this and this and that’s why you’re not in the squad”,’ Kane once told Daily Mail Sport. ‘And it just hit me. This is what I’ve got to do.’

Equally, the 54-year-old trades in subtlety. At Tottenham, he would sit at the entrance to the training ground canteen to gauge his players’ state of mind as they walked in. He had staff video them at training and wondered why they always looked happier when they walked off at the end.

At Tottenham, Pochettino would sit at the entrance to the training ground canteen to gauge his players’ state of mind as they walked in

Pochettino’s friendship with Sir Alex Ferguson is more than a decade old and endures. Ferguson will be thrilled at the appointment

As strange as it sounds, Pochettino chose the detergent in the washing room as he believed the smell of the first team kit was important. He dropped a player simply because he had noticed him eating stodgy food before sessions and another because he believed his choice of car to be inappropriate to his relative lowly standing in the game.

These are the kinds of things that look clever when you win and like new-age bunkum when you don’t. At Spurs, Pochettino’s results spoke for him but what is critical now is what version has walked through the door at Old Trafford.

It’s true that, to a large extent, we all view him as Pochettino 2016. In the decade that has followed, there have been underwhelming spells at Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea. His attempts at making the kind of emotional connections he thrives on in Paris, for example, soon ran into a brick wall with the words ‘Neymar’ and ‘Mbappe’ written on it.

To return to the Ferguson link again, Pochettino has not previously been shy of perceived similarities.

‘Ferguson used to tell his players that working hard is a talent,’ he wrote in his 2017 book Brave New World. ‘To me, if a player doesn’t work hard for the team, he won't play. Nothing happens by chance.’

What manager in football doesn’t value basic endeavour? Not one but, as mutual trust and shared belief starts to wane during a run of bad results, even the basics can get lost. With this in mind and with Pochettino’s energy and charisma in the building, it’s not unrealistic to expect a new manager bounce at Old Trafford.

His relationship with Fernandes will be crucial and the Portuguese should not expect the captaincy to be a given. At Tottenham, Pochettino gave it to his goalkeeper, Hugo Lloris.

Pochettino knows that coaches can’t speak to players the way they used to, or indeed may wish to. A greater degree of emotional intelligence is required.

Fernandes and Lisandro Martinez - both publicly critical of the set-up at United this season - can expect private words of advice from their new boss

Pochettino arrives at Old Trafford a wiser manager for working amid the background noise at Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea

United’s players can therefore expect WhatsApp messages at 11pm at night – sometimes including attachments of training clips – quiet words of advice or observation when passing their manager in a corridor or even a short note, serious or otherwise, left in a dressing room locker. How the likes of Fernandes, Cunha, Rashford, Harry Maguire and Lisandro Martinez respond to all this will be key.

So, too, will Pochettino’s ability or otherwise to make the best of the clunky chain of executive command that sits above him. At Tottenham, Pochettino and chairman Daniel Levy hit a sweet spot that wasn’t to last but for a time saw them so in tune they even took a horse-riding trip together. It was a synchronicity that electrified the whole football club.

Here in Manchester in 2026-27, it will feel different. At United, senior players criticise executives to the media while the fans wave green-and-gold scarves on matchday and sing unpleasant songs about not one but two different ownership groups. None of that will go away just because yet another manager is through the door.

Pochettino may feel he has some experience of such background noise from his time at PSG and indeed Chelsea. Equally, much of what happens over the course of the rest of this season and, if he is lucky, beyond will depend on his own reserves of energy, desire and self-regeneration. Does his own well remain deep enough?

The man who swept into Southampton with little-to-no English but bags of ideas and energy in January 2013 was an irresistible force of nature and he ran hot through the Premier League for a while. If he brings some of that to Old Trafford then he has a chance of making an impression at least.

But Pochettino’s take on Murderball, punishment laps and the infamous ‘Gacon’ 5km running drill he has been known to use may have to wait until the summer. United’s immediate issues, he will find, are more about a failing culture, centring less on playing style and more on emotional substance.

#1246. Structural and regulatory evolution across the genus Hordeum

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The genus Hordeum comprises cultivated barley and its wild relatives, an evolutionarily, ecologically and agriculturally important group of grasses1,2. Here we generated a chromosome-scale comparative genomic resource comprising all recognized diploid Hordeum species together with representative polyploid lineages. Comparative analyses reveal extensive structural variation, including inversions and chromosomal rearrangements that disrupt proximal collinearity and reflect lineage-specific genome remodelling. Single-copy gene phylogenies identify ancient hybridization, segmental exchange and introgression, revealing pervasive reticulate evolution during Hordeum diversification. We uncover widespread horizontal gene transfer from Panicoideae grasses into Hordeum, with many transferred genes showing evidence of transcription and functional integration. Retrotransposon proliferation explains genome size variation and provides insights into polyploid genome evolution. Whole-genome alignments reveal contrasting evolutionary dynamics: whereas coding sequences remain highly conserved, regulatory elements undergo rapid turnover, providing a rich source of regulatory diversity for phenotypic evolution. Case studies of vernalization and glume development demonstrate how natural variation in regulatory and coding sequences contributes to flowering time and floral morphology. This comprehensive pangenomic framework establishes Hordeum as a model for studying genome evolution, structural variation and the genetic basis of adaptive traits, offering new avenues for barley improvement.

The genus Hordeum comprises approximately 33 species and is widely distributed across the temperate regions of Eurasia and the Americas1,2,3. Hordeum is classified into two subgenera based on cytogenetic evidence: one containing the H and Xu genomes and the other containing the I and Xa genomes4. The basic chromosome number is seven, and, although most species are diploid, tetraploid and hexaploid taxa have also been described. Cultivated barley (Hordeum vulgare) is the best known and most extensively studied species, as it represents one of the earliest domesticated cereal crops. Today, barley is the world’s fourth most important grain, valued for its use in food, animal feed and brewing5. Cultivated barley and its wild progenitor (H. vulgare subsp. spontaneum) constitute a single inter-fertile gene pool, allowing for frequent gene flow between wild and cultivated forms6. This primary gene pool has long been exploited by breeders to introduce desirable traits6. Hordeum bulbosum has contributed valuable disease resistance genes through introgression7,8,9,10 due to its ability to hybridize directly with cultivated barley. The other Hordeum species are not domesticated but have important ecological and agricultural roles in ecosystem stability, environmental adaptation and forage use11,12,13,14,15. Together, Hordeum is both an agronomically important genus and a powerful model for studying crop evolution, environmental adaptation and resistance to biotic and abiotic stresses. Factors such as incomplete lineage sorting, recurrent hybridization and gene flow partly obscure species boundaries, leaving major evolutionary questions unresolved1,2,4,16,17. Recent barley pangenomes have substantially advanced our understanding of genomic variation within cultivated barley and its closest relatives10,18,19. However, these studies were largely confined to two species (H. vulgare and H. bulbosum) and therefore could not resolve genome-wide evolutionary processes operating across the genus, including the origin of large-scale structural variation, ancient hybridization, polyploid genome evolution and the diversification of regulatory loci. Extending comparative genomic analyses to encompass the entire genus is therefore essential to capture the full breadth of diversity within the Hordeum gene pool and to facilitate both evolutionary studies and the effective utilization of wild germplasm for barley improvement. Pangenomics now offers comprehensive resources to address such complexity. In crops such as tomato, potato, maize, grapevine, citrus and cotton, genus-level pangenomes have uncovered extensive structural variations, gene presence–absence and evolutionary dynamics20,21,22,23,24. Investigating structural variations helps to explain evolutionary processes and can inform crop breeding strategies25. However, the full extent of structural variation within Hordeum remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we generated chromosome-scale genome assemblies representing all recognized diploid Hordeum species together with representative polyploid lineages. This comparative genomic framework provides a view of structural and regulatory genome evolution across the genus, yielding new insights into genome evolution and establishing a foundation for the utilization of wild diversity in barley improvement.

To maximize phylogenetic representation across the genus, we selected 27 accessions representing 24 Hordeum species, encompassing all recognized diploid genome groups1 together with representative tetraploid and hexaploid lineages (Extended Data Fig. 1a, Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Figs. 1–25). The dataset comprises 22 diploid accessions, 4 tetraploid accessions and 1 hexaploid accession. Twenty-four genome sequences were assembled using PacBio HiFi accurate long reads and Hi-C data (Supplementary Tables 2 and 3 and Supplementary Figs. 26–28), using the TRITEX pipeline26,27. The sequence assemblies of H. vulgare and H. bulbosum were sourced from our previous work10,28. The previously published chromosome-level assembly of Hordeum marinum H559 (ref. 29) was updated using the TRITEX pipeline, and previously published transcriptome data, Bionano optical maps and Hi-C data of Hordeum erectifolium NGB6816 were used30. The average contig N50 of the assemblies is 39.24 Mb. Assembly sizes range from 2.90 Gb to 4.48 Gb (mean, 3.92 Gb) in diploid species and from 7.49 Gb to 8.56 Gb (mean, 8.16 Gb) in tetraploid species, whereas the single hexaploid genome has an assembly size of 10.90 Gb. Chloroplast genome assemblies range from 136,335 bp to 137,079 bp (mean, 136,840 bp) (Supplementary Table 1). High assembly quality is supported by an average long terminal repeat (LTR) assembly index (LAI) of 14.79, a consensus quality value (QV) of 67.30 and k-mer completeness of 97.22% (Supplementary Table 4). For the heterozygous diploid species H. bulbosum, the two phased haplotypes were designated as Hap1 and Hap2. For polyploid species, independently assembled chromosome sets derived from different ancestral genomes were defined as subgenomes and denoted as Sub1, Sub2 and Sub3 according to their phylogenetic relationships with diploid progenitor lineages (Fig. 1a). To assess the gene content in the Hordeum pangenome, we annotated all genomes using transcriptome data (Methods and Supplementary Tables 5 and 6). A gene consolidation method was applied to ensure high comparability of gene predictions, including those for Hordeum parodii (6x) and Hordeum gussoneanum (4x). The number of high-confidence gene models identified ranges from 35,573 for diploid Hordeum murinum to 94,943 for hexaploid H. parodii (Supplementary Table 7). We assessed the quality of the Hordeum gene annotations using BUSCO (v5.8.0) with the poales_odb12 dataset, comprising 6,282 near-universal single-copy orthologues from Poales. On average, 97.35% of BUSCO genes were identified as complete, 0.69% as fragmented and 1.84% as missing (Supplementary Table 7). Independent benchmarking with OMArk and PSAURON further confirmed the high completeness and overall quality of the gene annotations (Supplementary Table 7). Transposable element (TE) annotation using the panEDTA pipeline31 revealed that transposons constituted on average 86.12% of the genome, ranging from 83.27% to 90.35% (Supplementary Table 8).

a, Phylogenetic tree of Hordeum species. Sorghum bicolor, Oryza sativa, Brachypodium distachyon and Triticum monococcum were used as outgroups. Divergence times were inferred using 4DTV sites from genome-wide single-copy genes after excluding genomic regions with strong phylogenetic discordance (nRF > 0.21) identified in Extended Data Fig. 6c. Coloured rectangles represent different genome groups. Hap1 and Hap2 represent phased haplotypes of heterozygous diploid H. bulbosum, and Sub1, Sub2 and Sub3 indicate distinct ancestral subgenomes in polyploid species. The background colours represent the genome groups of the species in the following order from top to bottom: I, Xa, H, Xu and outgroup species. b, GENESPACE synteny plot among 34 Hordeum haplomes and four outgroup genomes. Grey bars represent chromosomes arranged by genomic position. For visualization purposes, the chromosomes of the smaller outgroup genomes (S. bicolor, O. sativa and B. distachyon) were proportionally enlarged by a factor of five. c, Dot plot comparisons of chromosome 4H across genomes diverged at different times. Two species were randomly selected from each phylogenetic node for sequence alignment (Supplementary Table 11). Six representative comparisons are shown, with the remaining comparisons presented in Extended Data Fig. 3a. The number displayed at the top of each alignment represents the estimated divergence time between the species shown on the x axis and those shown on the y axis.

Based on the annotated gene sets of all species, we constructed a gene-based Hordeum pangenome. Overall, 42.4% of genes were classified as core genes, 56.5% as shell genes and 1.1% as cloud genes (Extended Data Fig. 1b,c). Gene ontology enrichment analysis showed that phosphorylation- and kinase-related functions were enriched among core genes, ATP and RNA binding were enriched among shell genes, and defence response and oxidative stress response were enriched among cloud genes (Supplementary Fig. 29). Nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) genes are key components of the plant immune system and have essential roles in resistance to fungal and other pathogens32,33. A map of their diversity is critical for advancing our understanding of disease resistance mechanisms in crops. Analysis of NLR genes revealed that I genome species contain significantly more NLR genes than the other Hordeum genome groups (Welch’s t-test, P = 1.8 × 10−6) (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). To further characterize this diversity, we constructed an NLR pangenome across Hordeum haploid genome equivalents (haplomes), comprising 800 orthogroups, of which 13.75% were classified as core, 27.75% as shell and 58.50% as cloud gene families (Extended Data Fig. 2c). In addition, NLR gene clusters were significantly less abundant on chromosomes 4H and 5H than on the remaining chromosomes (Wilcoxon test, P < 2.2 × 10−16) (Extended Data Fig. 2d). Similarly, genome-wide analyses of pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) proteins and mitochondrial transcription termination factors (mTERFs) revealed significant expansions of restorer-of-fertility-like (RFL) subgroups in the I and Xa genome groups relative to the H and Xu genome groups. Because RFL proteins are involved in fertility restoration in plants carrying cytoplasmic male sterility (CMS)34, these expansions suggest that the smaller RFL repertoires of the H and Xu genome groups are derived rather than ancestral (Supplementary Fig. 30a–e and Supplementary Table 9). Expansion of RFL-PPRs was most pronounced in the I genome group, whereas RFL-mTERFs were significantly expanded in both the I and Xa genome groups. Notably, RFL-mTERF genes clustered on the short arm of chromosome 6H exhibited extensive copy-number variation between Xa–I and H–Xu genome groups (t-test, P = 5.2 × 10−6) (Supplementary Fig. 30f). This region includes the Rfm3 locus, which partially restores fertility in plants carrying the msm1 cytoplasm used in hybrid barley breeding35 (Supplementary Fig. 30g).

To assess the feasibility of graph-based pangenome analyses across highly diverged Hordeum genomes, we constructed a pangenome graph using Progressive Cactus and hal2vg, comprising 2.53 billion nodes and 3.46 billion edges (68.7 Gb). Approximately 68% of nodes represented single-base variants, illustrating the extensive sequence divergence captured by the graph. Although computationally intensive tasks such as indexing remained infeasible (Methods), we successfully performed global analyses of core, shell and cloud sequence content, graph saturation, sequence conservation and variant diversity (Supplementary Figs. 31–34). These results demonstrate both the potential of graph-based approaches for genus-wide comparative genomics and the need for more scalable methods for graph exploration and interpretation.

Previous studies have inferred the evolutionary relationships among Hordeum species from plastome and partial gene sequences1,17. However, the relationships among some species remained weakly supported. In this study, we reconstructed a maximum-likelihood tree using a genome-wide single-copy gene set. Unlike previous phylogenies1,17, our species tree resolved all major evolutionary relationships with maximum bootstrap support, particularly among the recently diverged I-genome species (Supplementary Fig. 35). To further evaluate the robustness of these relationships, we reconstructed an independent coalescent-based species tree using ASTRAL-Pro3 (Supplementary Fig. 36), which integrates individual maximum-likelihood gene trees, and a genome-wide phylogeny inferred by CASTER from whole-genome multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) (Supplementary Figs. 37 and 38). We also estimated the divergence times of these species using fourfold degenerate third-codon transversion (4DTV) sites, excluding genomic regions identified as putatively derived from ancient hybridization (Supplementary Table 13). We estimated the divergence time between H and Xu at 10.3 million years ago (Ma), whereas I and Xa diverged around 9 Ma. The crown-group age of Hordeum dates back approximately 12.27 Ma (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 10). The chromosomes of Triticeae species exhibit high collinearity at their distal chromosome regions36, which is also the case in Hordeum (Fig. 1b). However, when aligned, the proximal regions show substantial loss of collinearity and highly fragmented alignments. Whole-genome comparisons across Hordeum species revealed that chromosomal rearrangements accumulated progressively with evolutionary divergence, contributing to the loss of collinearity and increasingly fragmented alignments in proximal chromosomal regions (Fig.1c, Extended Data Fig. 3a, Supplementary Figs. 39–44 and Supplementary Table 11). Quantification of reverse-orientation alignments across all Hordeum haplomes further demonstrated that putative inversions accumulated significantly more rapidly in proximal than in distal chromosome regions during Hordeum evolution (Supplementary Fig. 45). Among the seven chromosomes, chromosome 4H exhibited the most extensive loss of proximal collinearity (Supplementary Table 12). Recently diverged species retained strong chromosome-scale collinearity despite the presence of numerous structural variants, whereas comparisons between the deeply diverged H–Xu and Xa–I genome groups (more than 9 Ma) showed almost complete fragmentation of proximal collinearity (Fig. 1c, Extended Data Fig. 3a and Supplementary Figs. 39–44). To estimate the size of non-collinear regions, we applied normalized coverage to identify these regions in species that diverged more than 9 Ma (Extended Data Fig. 3c,d, Supplementary Figs. 46–50 and Methods). In total, we determined the genome-wide distribution of non-collinear regions across chromosomes in Hordeum, with a cumulative size of 855 Mb identified in the H. vulgare genome (Supplementary Table 12). Given the central role of TEs in genome evolution, we compared TE composition between proximal and distal chromosome regions. Proximal regions contained a significantly higher proportion of TEs than distal regions (one-sided paired Wilcoxon test, P = 9.31 × 10−10), primarily due to an increased abundance of LTR/Gypsy retrotransposons (one-sided paired Wilcoxon test, P = 9.31 × 10−10) (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b and Supplementary Fig. 51). Together with the accumulation of large chromosomal rearrangements, these observations motivated a ‘stretch and twist’ model describing two complementary processes underlying the progressive loss of collinearity. The stretch component represents alignment displacement caused by TE amplification, whereas the twist component represents large-scale chromosomal rearrangements driven by structural variation (Extended Data Fig. 4c).

In contrast to the dynamic structural variations found in proximal regions, the distal regions displayed more conserved, shared structural variations. This highlights that the extensive loss of collinearity in proximal regions precludes reliable identification of structural variants across more distantly related Hordeum species. Notably, large structural variations in the distal regions were predominantly inversions. On chromosomes 3H and 7H, we identified two large inversions spanning nearly the entire chromosome and present in multiple species (Extended Data Fig. 4d). In total, 1,407 inversions larger than 2 Mb were identified across Hordeum species (Extended Data Fig. 4d). The construction of a comprehensive inversion map revealed six inversions on chromosome 1H that were unexpectedly shared across divergent phylogenetic lineages (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 5). We hypothesized that these large-scale structural variations might have originated from introgression events involving extensive chromosomal segments. We constructed a phylogenetic tree using the single-copy gene set from these regions to test this hypothesis. The resulting tree, resolved with maximum bootstrap support, confirmed that these structural variations are shared between one clade of the I genome group and the H–Xu genome groups (Fig. 2b). Moreover, 10 extant diploid Hordeum species diversified within 1.68 million years following the inferred hybridization event, whereas no comparable radiation occurred in other phylogenetic lineages during the same period (Figs. 1a and 2b and Extended Data Fig. 5). Notably, the alternative phylogenetic topology extends across contiguous chromosomal regions of approximately 200 Mb rather than isolated loci, indicating the inheritance of chromosome-scale haplotypes that are more consistent with ancient introgression than with stochastic gene tree discordance or incomplete lineage sorting.

The remaining genome comparisons are shown in Extended Data Fig. 5. To identify additional signatures of ancient hybridization across the genus, we developed a genome-wide scanning approach based on local phylogenetic discordance among single-copy genes. The single-copy gene set was partitioned into sliding windows, and normalized Robinson–Foulds (nRF) distance was calculated between local phylogenetic trees and the genome-wide species tree (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Peaks in nRF values indicate genomic regions with phylogenetic histories that deviate from the species tree and therefore represent candidate introgression events. Here, we define hybridization footprints as large chromosomal segments shared among multiple descendant species that consistently exhibit an alternative phylogenetic relationship relative to the genome-wide species tree. Using an empirical threshold of 0.21 derived from the genome-wide nRF distribution to distinguish discordance peaks from background variation (Extended Data Fig. 6b and Supplementary Fig. 52), we recovered the chromosome 1H hybridization signal, validating the genome-wide scanning approach. Additionally, we detected more than ten consecutive windows with strong phylogenetic discordance signals at multiple regions (Extended Data Fig. 6c and Supplementary Fig. 52). To further explore the underlying causes of these inconsistencies, we reconstructed local phylogenetic trees using the single-copy gene sets from these regions (Extended Data Fig. 6e,f, Supplementary Figs. 53–58 and Supplementary Table 13). Regions in which local phylogenies consistently supported a specific alternative relationship across a large chromosomal segment were interpreted as evidence of ancient hybridization. By comparing the regions that exhibited phylogenetic discordance with the whole-genome tree, we identified two large-scale segmental exchanges occurring within Hordeum jubatum, with maximum bootstrap support (Extended Data Fig. 6e,f and Supplementary Table 13). Surprisingly, this large-scale segmental exchange explains the major duplication and deletion pattern previously identified on chromosome 5H relative to the H. vulgare reference genome (Supplementary Figs. 12, 56, 59 and 60). The exchanged regions in the two H. jubatum subgenomes are each more closely related to different ancestral genomes, indicating that the apparent duplication and deletion resulted from ancestral segmental exchange rather than independent copy-number changes. (Extended Data Fig. 6d). In the allotetraploid H. gussoneanum, extensive segmental exchanges were detected between the two subgenomes on chromosomes 2, 5 and 7 (Extended Data Fig. 6e, Supplementary Figs. 53, 55 and 57 and Supplementary Table 13). In the allohexaploid H. parodii, subgenome 1 carried a large chromosomal segment on chromosome 7 derived from Hordeum stenostachys, whereas subgenomes 2 and 3 exhibited an additional segmental exchange on chromosome 4 (Extended Data Fig. 6f, Supplementary Figs. 54, 55 and 58 and Supplementary Table 13). Together, these megabase-scale structural variants preserve signatures of ancient interspecific hybridization and large-scale chromosomal exchange that are not evident from genome-wide phylogenies alone, providing new insights into the complex evolutionary history of Hordeum.

Genetic variation is essential for species evolution. Beyond sexual reproduction, horizontal gene transfer (HGT) serves as an evolutionary shortcut for acquiring novel genes. Traditionally considered rare in vascular plants, genomic advances have revealed widespread occurrences of HGT, challenging prior assumptions37,38. Our previous research demonstrated extensive HGT in Hordeum. Notably, species within section stenostachys (I genome; 16 out of 22 diploid species) possess ribosomal DNA (rDNA) acquired from grasses in the subfamily Panicoideae (for example, Panicum, Paspalum and Setaria)39,40. The oldest transfers (from Panicum), estimated to have occurred between 5 and 1.7 Ma, resulted in large genomic insertions on chromosome 5H, some spanning over 400 kb and containing TEs and protein-coding genes41. Here, we identified Panicoideae-derived nuclear genes across 20 diploid Hordeum species, with H. vulgare serving as a negative control39,41. Our analysis revealed 611 foreign genes that corresponded to 126 orthogroups, predominantly matching Paspalum (63%) and Panicum (22%) (Extended Data Fig. 7a and Supplementary Tables 14 and 15). The extent of HGT varied, with Hordeum flexuosum carrying the highest number of foreign genes (68 genes corresponding to 43 orthogroups) (Extended Data Fig. 7a). These findings align with studies indicating that grasses frequently exchange genetic material42,43. HGT frequency correlates with Hordeum phylogeny, with Mediterranean and West Asian species exhibiting fewer transferred genes than their South American counterparts. This supports the hypothesis that HGT has a cumulative impact on eukaryotic evolution44. The presence of a single panicoid gene in H. bulbosum and H. murinum can be explained by the introgression of chromosomal segment 1H from I genome species, rather than by an early HGT event predating the diversification of Hordeum (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 6c). Chromosomal mapping indicates that horizontally transferred genes are distributed across all seven Hordeum chromosomes, with chromosome 5H carrying the largest number (Extended Data Fig. 7b). These genes are significantly enriched in the distal regions of chromosome arms. Although distal regions generally contain higher local gene densities, negative binomial regression analysis showed that gene density explains only a small fraction of the observed variation in HGT abundance (pseudo-R2 = 0.034; Supplementary Fig. 61), indicating that higher gene density alone cannot account for the distal enrichment of HGT genes. Although co-transfer of genes remains uncertain, previous research suggests that large fragments of foreign DNA may be transferred together41,43. A substantial fraction (82 out of 126) of Panicoideae-derived orthogroups lack native Hordeum homologues, indicating novel gene acquisition. Functional annotation suggests that these genes may have roles in key physiological processes such as auxin transport, light response and transcription regulation. RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis detected at least one expressed HGT gene in 73 out of 126 orthogroups (Extended Data Fig. 7c and Supplementary Table 16). The potential adaptive significance of these genes warrants further investigation. Our genus-wide analysis establishes Hordeum as a model system for studying the evolutionary impact of HGT.

The genome assembly sizes of Hordeum species range from 2.90 Gb to 10.9 Gb and are highly correlated with previous flow-cytometric estimates45 (Fig. 3a). After accounting for the direct effects of polyploidization, the haplomes exhibit pseudomolecule sizes ranging from 2.85 Gb to 4.68 Gb. Apart from a 19 Mb duplication detected in the subgenome of H. jubatum, no large duplication events were identified (Supplementary Figs. 59–60). A strong correlation was observed between total TE content and haplome size (Fig. 3b), confirming that TE accumulation has significantly contributed to genome size variation in Hordeum. LTR retrotransposons were identified as the primary drivers of these changes, although DNA transposons also had a role (Fig. 3c). Correlation analyses of individual transposon superfamilies showed that multiple TE families contributed to genome size variation, although overall TE abundance remained the strongest predictor of haplome size (Supplementary Fig. 62a). We selected transposons annotated in the TREP database with an average content above 20 Mb and examined their variation across different Hordeum haplomes. These TE families clearly differentiated the major evolutionary lineages of Hordeum (Supplementary Fig. 62b). To investigate lineage-specific TE dynamics in greater detail, we focused on three LTR retrotransposon families (BARE1, Sabrina and BAGY2) and used TEpop46 to reconstruct their diversification histories. TE subfamilies correspond closely to the major Hordeum clades (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 8a,b), demonstrating lineage-specific amplification histories that contributed to genome size evolution.

Each dot represents one retrotransposon; colours indicate estimated insertion times (Ma). e, Distribution of insertion times of full-length LTR elements in H. jubatum, H. californicum and Hordeum roshevitzii. H. californicum and H. roshevitzii are the respective diploid progenitors of subgenomes 1 and 2 in H. jubatum1. f, Inference of post-allopolyploidization TE insertion dynamics in tetraploid H. murinum subsp. murinum (BCC 2009) based on full-length LTR/Copia elements shared between subgenomes.
